routes: Latin Quarter: 1807 cannonballs, Ørsted and the old library

Denmark's first waterworks, the Golden Horns corner and the walled-in British shot of 1807, Ørsted's discovery spot, the cast-iron book hall, the first Stolpersteine, Regensen's linden and the Round Tower library, ending at the Workers' Museum. About 2.5 km.
Slotsholmen to Kongens Nytorv: Lenin's room and the old bars

Nytorv's 1913 kiosk and green pissoir, Thorvaldsen's grave, the Kierkegaard statue, Lenin's reading room, then Nikolaj's pissoir, Bo-Bi, Café Dan Turèll, the McDonald's that replaced Kierkegaard's café and the 1723 cellar bar. About 2.5 km.

The 1910 Socialist International hall, the bullet holes of 9 April 1940, the citadel's command bunker, Willumsen's moved wooden temple, two 1807 cannonball sites in Østerbro, then the hall where the Øresund tunnel was cast. About 6 km.
Christianshavn, Christiania and Holmen to Refshaleøen

Kiosk No. 1, the cannonballs that really landed in Christianshavn, the unmarked post-war execution pad on the ramparts, the 1751 masting crane, then the B&W shipyard halls and the welding hall that is now Copenhagen Contemporary. About 4.5 km.
Nørrebro to Ryvangen: Assistens, Panum and Bohr

The rail-trail bridge, the cemetery of Kierkegaard, Andersen and Bohr, the brutalist Panum, Bohr's Auditorium A, the listed kiosk, a sea-mark church, then the execution ground at Ryvangen. About 8 km; bike it if you can.
Frederiksberg and Vesterbro: Shellhus to Vestre Kirkegård

The Gestapo HQ site and the school hit by mistake in the same raid, Lenin's lodging, Kierkegaard's café in Frederiksberg Gardens, the lab that gave us pH, Denmark's largest cemetery and a locomotive workshop. About 5.5 km.
Lyngby and Gentofte: concrete church, fort and Mariebjerg
Denmark's first concrete church, the biggest 1880s ring fort, Brandt's grid of grave rooms, Hadid's wing at Ordrupgaard and the kiosk at Bakken. About 8 km.
Bagsværd, Farum and Værløse by bike
An early concrete fort, Utzon's cloud vault, the corten megastructure at Farum, then the runway and shelters of the Cold War airbase. About 16 km by bike.
Western suburbs: Exner, Vestvolden, the prison and Rømer

The Exners' brick cave at Islev, the Nike command bunker in Vestvolden, Glostrup's crematorium, the closed Vridsløselille Prison, another Exner church and Rømer's observatory in the woods. About 17 km; bike or S-train.
Amager by bike: Amagerbanen to the Nike sites
The old Amager railway, Kastrup Fort, Dragør's last water posts and its fort, then the Nike radar fort at Kongelunden and the missile magazines on the common.
Køge Bay: Avedøre, ARKEN and Mosede
The walled welfare town of Avedøre, the concrete ark of a museum on the beach, then the First World War fort and museum.
North Zealand: royal milestones to Gilleleje
Two of the King's Road milestones and the 1584 paved road, the sealed nuclear bunker in the forest, then Gilleleje's October 1943 trail.
The 65 m deep lime quarry from its rim, the 1901 power station that is now Moderna Museet, then Östra kyrkogården and Lewerentz's last building.
The 600-year-old automaton clock, Strindberg's morning walk in the botanical garden, then Lewerentz's St Petri, where no brick was cut.

sights.name: Farum Midtpunkt
sights.blurb: 1970–75 corten-and-concrete megastructure, about 1,600 social homes ('Rustenborg'), with first-floor access streets and vast parking decks underneath.
sights.when: Lived-in social housing; public paths are open. Be discreet with cameras. S-train to Farum.

sights.name: Avedøre Stationsby and Store Hus
sights.blurb: A planned welfare town ringed by a continuous housing 'town wall' with gates, modelled on Dubrovnik; Store Hus, a 464-flat slab, stands at the station.
sights.when: Public streets and park; homes, so be discreet. S-train Avedøre.

sights.name: Panum Institute
sights.blurb: Comb-shaped mass of concrete, brick and brown steel (1971–86), Copenhagen's archetypal brutalist campus; the stepped Tagensvej wall was built against a motorway never built.
sights.when: University building; the street perimeter is free. Visitors report a free view lounge on the 15th floor of the Mærsk Tower (unverified).

sights.name: Vridsløselille Prison (closed)
sights.blurb: Walled 1859 prison emptied in 2015–16: dungeons, security cells, isolation yards, church and workshops, shown by former staff before redevelopment.
sights.when: Guided tours only: Porten tours Sat–Sun 12:00 and 14:30, 165 kr (Sept 2026 listing). Ages 12+, not step-free. Book ahead.

sights.name: Bagsværd Church (Utzon)
sights.blurb: Utzon's 'grain silo': a plain tiled box around a billowing in-situ concrete vault, completed 1976. In the Danish Culture Canon.
sights.when: Free. Tue–Fri 10–14, Sun and holidays 12–16; Saturdays only 1 Apr–30 Sep. Closed Mon and during ceremonies. Call 48 h ahead: 44 98 41 41.

sights.name: Sankt Knud Lavard Church
sights.blurb: Denmark's first pure concrete church (1956–57) in Lyngby: béton-brut walls, freestanding concrete campanile, glass-block choir wall. Listed as a precursor of Bagsværd.
sights.when: Active Catholic parish with no published visiting hours: go around Mass (visitors mention English Mass on Sundays at 12:00, unverified) or contact the parish.
sights.q: Sankt Knud Lavard Kirke, Lyngbygårdsvej 1A, 2800 Kongens Lyngby

sights.name: Lundehus Church
sights.blurb: Slate-clad pyramid on a triangular plot with an open bell chamber at the tip like a sea-mark; whitewashed concrete rafters inside (1957).
sights.when: Parish church; hours not published. Google lists Tue–Fri 10–13 (unverified).

sights.name: Islev Church (Exner)
sights.blurb: Inger and Johannes Exner's rough-brick cave (1969–70): a dark nave lit from skylights, entered through a forest of forged-iron columns.
sights.when: Parish church; hours not published. Google lists Tue–Fri 10–13 (unverified).

sights.name: Opstandelseskirken, Albertslund
sights.blurb: A late Exner church (1984) with landscape by Lea Nørgård, a short walk from Vridsløselille Prison.
sights.when: Some weekday 09:00 services; Google lists weekday daytime hours (unverified). Weekends likely closed.

sights.name: Mariebjerg Cemetery
sights.blurb: G.N. Brandt's 1936 grid of square 'grave rooms', each with its own planting, plus Schlegel's concrete chapel-crematorium. In the Danish Culture Canon.
sights.when: Open sunrise to sunset; free. Entrances from Lyngbyvejen and Nybrovej.

sights.name: Glostrup Crematorium and Chapel
sights.blurb: 1960 decorative-brick crematorium by Selchau, Brüel, Bornebusch and Henning Larsen, with a copper entrance and a large skylight.
sights.when: Working cemetery and crematorium; be discreet during ceremonies. A new crematorium next to it was reported under construction (unverified).
sights.q: Glostrup Krematorium og Kapel, Gamle Landevej 1, 2600 Glostrup

sights.name: Östra kyrkogården and Lewerentz's flower kiosk, Malmö
sights.blurb: Malmö's largest cemetery, shaped by Sigurd Lewerentz from 1917 to 1969, with his last, most stripped-down building: a 1969 concrete flower kiosk at the gate.
sights.when: Cemetery open daily. The kiosk closes at 17:00 (Skissernas Museum), so come in daylight.

sights.name: St Petri Church, Klippan (Lewerentz)
sights.blurb: An 18 × 18 m dark brick room on a T-shaped iron cross, where Lewerentz allowed no brick to be cut; the font is a giant shell on a rock (1962–66).
sights.when: Free, open daily: Mon–Fri 08–18, Sat–Sun 10–18. Guided tours by arrangement (info@sanktpetrikyrka.se). About 1 h north of Malmö.

sights.name: Flyvestation Værløse runway
sights.blurb: Decommissioned NATO airbase: a 3 km by 50 m runway you can walk, cycle or skate, 1930s hangars and 12 hardened aircraft shelters. Fence-free since 2012.
sights.when: Free and open all day. Keep out of fenced National Museum areas. 20 km from the Town Hall Square.

sights.name: Værløse Air History Hangar (Hangar 2)
sights.blurb: Volunteer-run hangar of Danish Air Force aircraft at the old base; free, donations welcome.
sights.when: Tue 9–14 and Sat 13–16 (local listing; Google agrees). Free.

sights.name: Kastellet command bunker
sights.blurb: German standard staff bunker (Regelbau 608), the last big structure built in the citadel; Cold War war HQ for Greater Copenhagen.
sights.when: Citadel is a free public park. The bunker is a veterans' meeting place, open to all only on special days.

sights.name: Ejbybunkeren on Vestvolden
sights.blurb: Labyrinthine Cold War bunker dug into the 1880s Vestvolden rampart, the command bunker for Copenhagen's Nike air defence.
sights.when: Self-guided season (weekends and school holidays 11–16) likely ended after the autumn break; check vestvolden.dk. Group tours year-round. The rampart is free.

sights.name: Kongelundsfortet
sights.blurb: 1914–16 coastal fort that became the radar and fire-control site of Nike squadron 532 (1959–81): radar platforms, casemate, bunker, 1980s air-watch tower.
sights.when: Owned by Dragør Kommune as an outdoor centre; open 08–20 daily, free.

sights.name: Nike magazines, Kalvebod Fælled
sights.blurb: Three surviving Nike missile magazine buildings on the open common, with the launch sites visible; munitions bunkers reported open.
sights.when: Public common, free. Pin is rough (about 1 km); status is from a 2020 report.

sights.name: Garderhøjfortet
sights.blurb: Largest fort of Copenhagen's 1880s land fortifications, with Experimentarium-designed exhibitions and a working 15 cm gun.
sights.when: Weekends and holidays 10:30–16; adults 80 kr. The gun fires on the last Sunday of the month at 12:00: next is 25 Oct.

sights.name: Bagsværdfortet
sights.blurb: Early reinforced-concrete fort (1892–93), reportedly the only one with intact storm railings, plus an observation tower.
sights.when: Grounds free. The tower opens only on Fæstningsdagen in late September (per TripAdvisor).

sights.name: Kastrup Fort
sights.blurb: 1886–87 sea-front fort, decommissioned 1922 and closed by the Germans 1940–47; now a protected park with large earthworks.
sights.when: Free daytime access; dogs on lead, no cycling. A restaurant operates inside.
sights.q: Kastrup Fort, Amager Strandvej 246, 2300 København S

sights.name: Dragør Fort
sights.blurb: 1910–15 fort: a German gunnery school in WWII and a coastal radar station until 2001, with views to the Øresund Bridge.
sights.when: Grounds open (Google lists 06–21); restaurant, hotel and events are private. No own food and drink.
sights.q: Dragør Fort, Prins Knuds Dæmning 2, 2791 Dragør

sights.name: Mosede Fort (Danmark 1914–18 museum)
sights.blurb: First World War fort on Køge Bay with a museum about Denmark's neutrality in 1914–18.
sights.when: Tue–Fri 11–15, Sat–Sun 11–16, closed Mon. Adults 110 kr, under-18 free. Free intro tour at 12:00.

sights.name: Middelgrundsfort
sights.blurb: 1890–94 artificial sea fort, called the world's largest; military until 1984, now a scouts' youth island.
sights.when: Seasonal boats only (Spar Shipping), about 35 min from Nyhavn. Save for spring or summer.

sights.name: Flakfortet
sights.blurb: 1910–16 sea fort on concrete caissons cast at Lynetten and floated out; for sale in 2026, price cut from 74.75 to 42 million kr.
sights.when: Off-season: ferries ran from 25 Apr 2026 (no Mondays); the restaurant usually closes in late September. Ownership may change.

sights.name: Cold War Museum Stevnsfort
sights.blurb: 1.7 km of tunnels 18 m inside the UNESCO cliff of Stevns Klint, guarding the southern Øresund 1950s–2000 with HAWK and Nike missiles on top.
sights.when: Underground by guided tour only (24 per tour, book at oesm.dk); ticket includes the grounds. About 1 h by car. Third-party hours conflict.

sights.name: Gurre bunker (BOC1)
sights.blurb: Denmark's first nuclear-proof government bunker (1958–61) under a concrete 'tortoise shell', decorated by Poul Gernes; sealed.
sights.when: Permanently sealed since a one-off 2013 opening; only the fenced entrance in Krogenberg Hegn is visible.

sights.name: Tunnelfabrikken, Nordhavn
sights.blurb: The 261 m hall where the Øresund tunnel elements were cast in the 1990s, one of Denmark's largest buildings; free museum and café inside.
sights.when: Free museum, most likely Wed–Fri 10–14 (one listing says Tue–Thu). The hall is to be raised and rebuilt with about 400 homes, so go soon.

sights.name: Refshaleøen (former B&W shipyard)
sights.blurb: 125 years of Burmeister & Wain shipbuilding (to 1996): 1960s section halls, the welding hall (now Copenhagen Contemporary), the dry dock and the 'steel line'.
sights.when: Free to wander. Current uses are assumed until 2031; masterplan proposals were published in May 2026.

sights.name: Limhamn lime quarry, Malmö
sights.blurb: A 1,300 × 800 m, 65 m deep abandoned limestone pit (worked 1866–1994), kept dry by pumping; seen from a 4 km rim trail.
sights.when: Rim trail always open and free (viewpoints, binoculars). The pit floor is guided-entry only via Malmö stad. Bus stop Kalkbrottet.

sights.name: Nørrebroruten and Åbuen
sights.blurb: Copenhagen's landscaped Petite Ceinture: about 8.5 km of path on the inner freight railway closed in 1930, crossing the city on the Åbuen bridge.
sights.when: Public path, always open. Prize-winning (Byplanprisen 2013).

sights.name: Amagerbanen remnants
sights.blurb: Surviving freight yard and track of the old Amager railway (passengers to 1938, closed by 1995), with volunteer rail-bikes on about 500 m of track.
sights.when: Track and path always visible. Rail-bike days not verified for 2026; visitors say it is free and not open every day.

sights.name: Cannonball at Kommunitetsbygningen
sights.blurb: A cannonball walled into the university building beside its gate, plus tablets for the city fires of 1641 and 1728: bombardment relic and fire memorial on one wall.
sights.when: University courtyard, generally open on weekday daytimes; free. Look on both the Magnoliegården and Nørregade sides.

sights.name: Cannonballs at Nørregade 11 and 13
sights.blurb: Balls above the Bispegården gate (no. 11) and over the gate at no. 13; the no. 13 balls are from the 1659 Swedish siege, found in a 1900s rebuild.
sights.when: Street facades; free.

sights.name: Cannonball at Teglgårdstræde 14
sights.blurb: A ball at first-floor height behind a downpipe, one of the cluster walled in after the 1807 bombardment.
sights.when: Street facade; free. Look up behind the downpipe.

sights.name: Cannonball at Sankt Gertruds Stræde 6
sights.blurb: A ball above the gate of a 1736 house that survived the 1807 bombardment.
sights.when: Street facade; free.

sights.name: Cannonball in Larsbjørnsstræde 7A courtyard
sights.blurb: A ball on the rear building in the courtyard of no. 7A, in the old Pisserenden quarter.
sights.when: Courtyard; depends on the gate being open (often daytime only).

sights.name: Cannonball in the Main Library courtyard
sights.blurb: A ball left of the door of a surviving rear house in the courtyard of Hovedbiblioteket, Krystalgade 15. The 'it hit right here' story is almost certainly false.
sights.when: Library courtyard, usually open in library hours.

sights.name: Cannonballs at KVUC, Vognmagergade
sights.blurb: Several balls of different sizes on the former lighting-department headquarters at the Vognmagergade/Landemærket corner.
sights.when: Street corner; free.

sights.name: Cannonballs at Jennows Gård, Christianshavn
sights.blurb: A couple of balls in the gateway of Strandgade 12; Christianshavn was mostly out of range, so these may really have landed nearby.
sights.when: Street gateway; free. Single blog source, unverified.

sights.name: Unknown cannonball, Randersgade 8
sights.blurb: A ball above the entrance in Østerbro that the local guide calls an 'unknown cannonball', 'probably' from 1807.
sights.when: Street facade; free. Origin undocumented.

sights.name: Livjægerne plaque with two cannonballs
sights.blurb: Plaque over a gate for the Royal Life Jägers' part in the 1807 sortie at Classens Have, flanked by two balls from the fight.
sights.when: Holsteinsgade area; exact building not confirmed. Pin is the street only.

sights.name: Amalienborg bullet holes (9 April 1940)
sights.blurb: Bullet scars from the Royal Life Guards' fight with German infantry on the morning of the invasion; fire ceased at 05:55, Denmark capitulated at 06:00.
sights.when: Public square, always open; free. Sources don't pinpoint the marks: look on the Ny Toldbodgade/Amaliegade side.

sights.name: Shellhuset memorial tablets
sights.blurb: The rebuilt office on the exact site of the Gestapo HQ destroyed by RAF Mosquitos on 21 March 1945, with Danish and RAF memorial tablets.
sights.when: Street facade; free.

sights.name: French School memorial (Institut Jeanne d'Arc)
sights.blurb: Max Andersen's 1953 mourning mother on the site of the school hit by mistake in the Shellhus raid; about 86 children were among the dead.
sights.when: Open-air, always accessible; free. Paving stones carry the names. Annual ceremony 21 March.
sights.q: Den Franske Skoles Plads, Frederiksberg Allé 74, 1820 Frederiksberg C

sights.name: Ryvangen execution ground (Mindelunden)
sights.blurb: Bronze copies of the three German execution posts where resistance fighters were shot in 1943–45, plus the Great Grave Field and Kaj Munk's lines.
sights.when: Daily; Oct 10–16, Nov–Dec 10–15. Free. Free public tours at weekends and on holidays, no booking. No dogs or bikes.

sights.name: Post-war execution shed remains, Christiania
sights.blurb: An unmarked 1 × 2 m concrete pad with a rusting drain grate on the 2nd redan: the base of the shed where 30 collaborators were shot in 1946–50.
sights.when: Open ground on the rampart path; free. No sign, and the pin is approximate (±300 m): look on the 2nd redan near Norddyssen 63.

sights.name: Gilleleje church loft and October 1943 plaques
sights.blurb: The church attic where the Gestapo seized hiding Jews on 6–7 October 1943, seven bronze story plaques round town, and Karin Lind's split stone 'Forskudt Horisont'.
sights.when: Plaques outdoor and free; a 2.1 km self-guided route exists. Church opening varies by season, so check if you want the loft.

sights.name: First Danish Stolpersteine, Krystalgade 12
sights.blurb: Three brass stones in front of the synagogue for residents of the Meyers Minde home, the first laid in Denmark (10 June 2019).
sights.when: Always visible; free. Full address lists at snublesten.dk.

sights.name: Ørsted's discovery of electromagnetism, Nørregade 21
sights.blurb: 'In a house on this site the physicist H.C. Ørsted discovered electromagnetism in 1820': inscription and a relief of Ørsted holding a wire over a compass.
sights.when: Street facade; free. The auditorium itself no longer exists.

sights.name: Carlsberg Laboratory, birthplace of pH
sights.blurb: The listed 1875 lab buildings where S.P.L. Sørensen introduced pH (1909) and Emil Chr. Hansen bred pure-culture lager yeast (1883); founder's statue in front.
sights.when: Working research centre; exterior from the street only. Free. No dedicated pH plaque confirmed.
sights.q: Carlsberg Laboratorium, Gamle Carlsberg Vej 10, 1799 København V

sights.name: Ole Rømer's Observatorium Tusculanum
sights.blurb: Stone-marked outline of Rømer's 1704 observatory hut, home of the world's first meridian circle, found in 1978 by a music teacher.
sights.when: Open woodland at the edge of Vestskoven, always accessible; free. Kroppedal Museum nearby has its own hours and fees.
sights.q: Observatorium Tusculanum, Ole Rømers Vej, 2630 Taastrup

sights.name: Telephone kiosk No. 1, Christianshavns Torv
sights.blurb: Fritz Koch's ornate copper-roofed kiosk, the first one (1896 or 1906), moved here from Kongens Nytorv; now a coffee kiosk.
sights.when: Exterior always visible. Visitors report it now sells coffee and buns.

sights.name: Listed telephone kiosk, Poul Henningsens Plads
sights.blurb: The only one of Koch's ten original kiosks still in its original place; listed in 1994 (or 1996).
sights.when: Exterior always visible; reportedly a café pavilion (verify). Pin is the square.

sights.name: Nytorv kiosk and green pissoir
sights.blurb: A 1913 kiosk still in place and a dark-green, fully screened cast-iron urinal: Copenhagen's answer to the vespasienne.
sights.when: Outdoor; free. The pissoir is assumed still standing (2016 source). Pin is the square.

sights.name: Green pissoir, Nikolaj Plads
sights.blurb: The second surviving green cast-iron pissoir, beside the former St Nicholas Church, now Nikolaj Kunsthal.
sights.when: Outdoor; free. Assumed still standing (2016 source).

sights.name: Kongens Nytorv kiosk
sights.blurb: A 1913-model kiosk on the square where kiosk No. 1 first stood, moved a few metres in the 2004 refurbishment.
sights.when: Outdoor; free. Pin approximate.

sights.name: Telephone kiosk at Dyrehavsbakken
sights.blurb: A Koch kiosk moved to Bakken from Store Kongensgade/Gernersgade, 10 minutes from Lyngby.
sights.when: Bakken has seasonal opening; the kiosk's current state is unverified. Pin is the park.

sights.name: Royal milestone on Lyngbyvej ('FV ¾ M')
sights.blurb: A protected red-granite three-quarter-mile stone with Frederik V's cipher, about 30 × 30 × 70 cm.
sights.when: Roadside, free. Pin approximate: the stone has likely moved in road widening, so verify the spot.

sights.name: Royal milestone, Hørsholm ('FV 3¼ M')
sights.blurb: A three-and-a-quarter-mile stone on the pedestrian street, by the optician, repainted by the local museum society.
sights.when: Roadside on the pedestrian street; free.

sights.name: Royal milestone and King's Road, Nyrup Hegn
sights.blurb: A 5½-mile Norwegian-marble obelisk with posthorn and Christian VII's monogram, plus walkable stretches of Frederik II's 1584 paved King's Road.
sights.when: Roadside in front of Naturcenter Nyruphus; free.

sights.name: Dragør's last street water posts
sights.blurb: Two of the town's nine public water posts survive on cobbled squares, from before the 1907 waterworks.
sights.when: Public squares (Hans Isbrandtsens Plads and Jens Eyberts Plads); free.

sights.name: Pumpehuset, Denmark's first waterworks
sights.blurb: Nebelong's 1859 yellow-brick engine house with round-arched cast-iron windows; ran until 1951, now a concert venue.
sights.when: Exterior always visible; inside only during concerts.

sights.name: Where the Golden Horns were melted
sights.blurb: An ordinary corner in the medieval grid where the goldsmith-forger Niels Heidenreich melted the stolen Golden Horns of Gallehus.
sights.when: Public street corner (Studiestræde/Larsbjørnsstræde); free. The exact building is not documented.

sights.name: Mastekranen (masting crane), Nyholm
sights.blurb: Philip de Lange's 1748–51 timber-and-brick sheer-leg crane for stepping masts into warships, facing the harbour.
sights.when: Visible from across the water and on Nyholm (naval area reported open). Visitors say you can ask at a ticket office for a guide to take you up (unverified).
sights.q: Mastekranen, A.H. Vedels Plads, 1439 København K

sights.name: Ven: Tycho Brahe's Stjerneborg
sights.blurb: Tycho's partly reconstructed underground observatory, the marked footprint of Uraniborg and his own pew in St Ibb's church.
sights.when: Museum season is over: 1 May–31 Aug daily, September weekends only. Ferries from Landskrona. Save for next summer.
sights.q: Tycho Brahe Museet, Landsvägen 182, Sankt Ibb, Ven

sights.name: Lund Cathedral's astronomical clock
sights.blurb: A c. 1425 automaton clock: knights clash on the hour, and at set times the Three Magi parade while a small organ plays 'In dulci jubilo'.
sights.when: Plays Mon–Sat 12:00 and 15:00, Sun 13:00 and 15:00; short talk Mon–Sat 11:45. Cathedral entry free.

sights.name: Gammel Læsesal, Royal Library (Lenin's seat)
sights.blurb: The 1906 reading room, still in use, where Lenin read in 1910 (lore says chair no. 9) and Georg Brandes worked. Green glass lamps.
sights.when: Students and researchers only, Mon–Sat. Free phone-off 'Læsesalon' evenings 11 Nov and 9 Dec, 16:30. Black Diamond tours are public.
sights.q: Det Kgl. Bibliotek, Søren Kierkegaards Plads 1, 1221 København K

sights.name: Auditorium A, Niels Bohr Institute
sights.blurb: The original 1921 lecture hall where Bohr, Heisenberg, Pauli, Dirac and Gamow argued out quantum mechanics; Bohr's office kept intact.
sights.when: Public tours suspended for renovation 'until further notice'. Get in via the Niels Bohr International Academy public lectures in Auditorium A, or email the Bohr Archive (sunderland@nbi.ku.dk).
sights.q: Niels Bohr Institutet, Blegdamsvej 17, 2100 København Ø

sights.name: Hviids Vinstue
sights.blurb: A dark, many-roomed cellar wine bar in the same rooms since 1723, drunk in by Royal Theatre actors. The Andersen medallion is a myth.
sights.when: Open daily, walk in. Smørrebrød at lunch, gløgg in winter.
sights.q: Hviids Vinstue, Kongens Nytorv 19, 1050 København K

sights.name: Workers' Museum festsal and Øl-Halle '1892'
sights.blurb: Europe's oldest workers' assembly building (1879): Stauning's office, the restored banquet hall, and Copenhagen's only listed basement tavern, where you can eat and drink.
sights.when: Museum daily 10–17, Thu to 20; adults 135 kr, ages 18–25 110 kr. Øl-Halle 11–17 (Parkmuseerne lists Tue–Sat). Lunch buffet about 299 kr.

sights.name: Det Lille Apotek
sights.blurb: Low cellar rooms with old paintings, marketed as Copenhagen's oldest restaurant (1720) where Andersen wrote The Ugly Duckling. The story doesn't hold.
sights.when: Lunch and dinner; booking advised. Go for the room, not the story.
sights.q: Det Lille Apotek, Store Kannikestræde 15, 1169 København K

sights.name: Bo-Bi Bar
sights.blurb: A tiny red-walled bodega since 1917 opposite the Gyldendal publishing house; smoking allowed, décor described as unchanged.
sights.when: Walk in. Smoking is allowed inside.

sights.name: Café Dan Turèll
sights.blurb: A Parisian-style café-bar from 1977 named after its regular, the writer Dan Turèll, who (legend says) traded his name for free food and drink.
sights.when: Open daily from morning. Recently renovated, partly into a cocktail and wine bar.
sights.q: Café Dan Turèll, Store Regnegade 3, 1110 København K

sights.name: House of Josty, Frederiksberg Gardens (Kierkegaard's café)
sights.blurb: The café site where Kierkegaard 'sat as usual and smoked my cigar' and decided to become an author; reopened in 2026, in an 1899 building.
sights.when: Tue–Fri 8–17, Sat–Sun 9–17; kitchen closes 15:00. Presumably closed Mon. Walk-ins welcome; tables at houseofjosty.com.
sights.q: House of Josty, Pile Allé 14A, 2000 Frederiksberg

sights.name: Library Hall, Round Tower
sights.blurb: The University Library's hall from 1657 to 1861, where the young Andersen was allowed to borrow books; now an exhibition and concert hall.
sights.when: Included in the Round Tower ticket. Rotating contemporary exhibitions.

sights.name: Old University Library, Fiolstræde 1
sights.blurb: Herholdt's 1861 cast-iron book hall, full of books on two levels; a library for 148 years, reopened in 2023 'not as a library, not as a museum'.
sights.when: Tue–Wed and Fri–Sat 10–16, Thu 10–20, closed Sun–Mon; 75 kr in 2023. Daily tours 13:00 (Danish) and 14:00 (English). Hours may have changed.

sights.name: Regensen courtyard and the linden
sights.blurb: A student college since 1623; its linden (first planted 1785) was the students' meeting point, and Studenterforeningen was founded under it in 1820.
sights.when: Private residence: glimpse through the gate. Open on Culture Night, at courtyard flea markets and for group tours (1,000 kr per hour).

sights.name: University main building, Frue Plads (Brandes 1871)
sights.blurb: Where Georg Brandes began his Main Currents lectures on 3 November 1871 'in auditorium 7', starting the Modern Breakthrough.
sights.when: Working university building; auditoriums open for public lectures and events. No standing exhibit.
sights.q: Københavns Universitet, Frue Plads, 1165 København K

sights.name: Odd Fellow Palæet (1910 Socialist International)
sights.blurb: Where the 8th International Socialist Congress met in 1910 with about 890 delegates, including Lenin, Rosa Luxemburg and Jean Jaurès.
sights.when: Private event and concert venue: inside only for a concert or event (candlelight concerts are common).
sights.q: Odd Fellow Palæet, Bredgade 28, 1260 København K

sights.name: Studenterhuset, Købmagergade 52
sights.blurb: Still a student café and bar; a plaque records Studenterforeningen's first rooms here, 1820–24.
sights.when: Walk in; cheap student bar.

sights.name: Botanical Garden, Lund (Strindberg's walk)
sights.blurb: Where Strindberg took his morning walk during his Inferno years in Lund (1896–99); free and open daily.
sights.when: Free, open daily. Greenhouse, café and toilets reported closed for renovation until 2027.

sights.name: Royal Library Garden (Kierkegaard statue)
sights.blurb: One of the city's quietest gardens, with Hasselriis' seated Kierkegaard. A memorial, not a haunt: the garden postdates him.
sights.when: Public garden; free.
sights.q: Det Kongelige Biblioteks Have, Proviantpassagen, 1218 København K

sights.name: Assistens Cemetery
sights.blurb: Nørrebro's cemetery-park, where locals read on the benches near the graves of Kierkegaard, Andersen and Bohr.
sights.when: Open daily (7–19 per the October listing). Free. Sunday 25 Oct 14:00: last of Christian Kronman's cemetery tours.

sights.name: Kierkegaard's café, now a McDonald's
sights.blurb: Mini's konditori, where Kierkegaard and Andersen sat, was torn down in 1857 for Café à Porta, which went bankrupt and became a McDonald's.
sights.when: Kongens Nytorv 17; walk in if you want. The original house is gone.

sights.name: Lenin's lodging plaque, Vesterbrogade 112
sights.blurb: The house where Lenin rented a back room during his 1910 stay; the plaque is in a locked back courtyard.
sights.when: House with a plaque in a locked courtyard; street only.

sights.name: Thorvaldsen's grave and museum courtyard
sights.blurb: Thorvaldsen is buried in the open courtyard of his own museum, Denmark's first public museum building (1848), among painted palms, lions and crocodiles.
sights.when: Museum closed Mondays, free on Wednesdays. The courtyard may be closed during the 2026–27 facade restoration.
sights.q: Thorvaldsens Museum, Bertel Thorvaldsens Plads 2, 1213 København K

sights.name: Den Frie Udstillingsbygning
sights.blurb: J.F. Willumsen's 1893 wooden temple of the arts with a gilded Pegasus, moved to Oslo Plads in 1898; one of the first Danish buildings made for exhibitions.
sights.when: Closed Mon–Tue; Wed, Fri 12–18, Thu 12–20, Sat–Sun 10–18. Between shows 2–6 Nov.
sights.q: Den Frie Udstillingsbygning, Oslo Plads 1, 2100 København Ø

sights.name: Lokomotivværkstedet
sights.blurb: A former DSB locomotive workshop in Sydhavn, now a hall for fairs and events.
sights.when: Event venue; inside only during events. Exterior any time.
sights.q: Lokomotivværkstedet, Otto Busses Vej 5A, 2450 København SV

sights.name: Vestre Kirkegård
sights.blurb: Denmark's largest designed cemetery; on Sat 31 Oct its Nordre Kapel hosts a free All Souls' 'Day of the Dead' afternoon.
sights.when: Open daily. 'De Dødes Dag' Sat 31 Oct 14–17 at Nordre Kapel (talk 15:00, names read 16:00), appears free.
sights.q: Vestre Kirkegård, Nordre Kapel, Vestre Kirkegårds Allé 15, 2450 København SV

sights.name: ARKEN Museum (building)
sights.blurb: Søren Robert Lund's ship-like concrete museum (1996) on the Køge Bay beach park.
sights.when: See Events for shows and hours. 16 Oct listing showed a 10–21 late opening.

sights.name: Ordrupgaard (Zaha Hadid extension)
sights.blurb: Art museum with Zaha Hadid's concrete extension and Finn Juhl's own house in the park.
sights.when: See Events: Snedkernes Efterårsudstilling opens 23 (or 24) Oct. About 15 min from Lyngby.

sights.name: Moderna Museet Malmö (1901 power station)
sights.blurb: John Smedberg's 1901 power station with Tham & Videgård's perforated orange extension.
sights.when: See Events. Free entry for under-25s reported by visitors (unverified).
sights.q: Moderna Museet Malmö, Ola Billgrens plats 2-4, Malmö

sights.name: Bellahøj point houses
sights.blurb: 28 free-standing point towers of 9–13 storeys on the Bellahøj ridge.
sights.when: Go soon: 10 of the 28 towers are approved for demolition, and stripping of the three empty Bellahøj Syd towers began in week 40 of 2026. The grounds are public; the towers are homes.

sights.name: Høje Gladsaxe
sights.blurb: Five 16-storey and two 9-storey slab blocks lined up as a wall on the hilltop above Utterslev Mose. The north side has deck-access walkways; the park side has the blue façades from the 1990s.
sights.when: Lived in, and the park is open. The north decks are best seen from the car parks.

sights.name: Tingbjerg and the Langhusvej rowhouses
sights.blurb: A yellow-brick "new town" of three-storey blocks. Its landmark is a 13-storey tower visible from Grundtvigs Kirke across Utterslev Mose. There are landscape spaces by C.Th. Sørensen.
sights.when: The Borgerrepræsentationen voted to demolish Steen Eiler Rasmussen's 42 Langhusvej rowhouses from 1970 and removed their preservation status, as part of the plan required by the parallel-societies law. Check whether they are still standing before you go.

sights.name: Herlev Vænge balconies
sights.blurb: Brick slab blocks from just after the war, with star patterns cast into the concrete balconies.
sights.when: Lived in and public from the street. The exact address and coordinates are unverified.

sights.name: Enghave Church: concrete bell tower
sights.blurb: Restrained red brick on the outside, a free-standing concrete bell tower with an open bell chamber and cross motifs between the two wings, and inside a bright concrete space with a flat barrel vault.
sights.when: Active parish church; the interior is open during services or opening hours, which were not checked.
sights.q: Enghave Kirke, Sønder Boulevard 120, 1720 København V

sights.name: Bispebjerg Cemetery and crematorium
sights.blurb: A strictly symmetrical plan from 1903 that has softened into parkland. Its poplar avenue continues the axis of Grundtvigs Kirke down to Utterslev Mose.
sights.when: Open, free.

sights.name: Dansekapellet (old crematorium dome)
sights.blurb: A domed crematorium building from the early 1900s, converted into a municipal dance house.
sights.when: An active Københavns Kommune venue. Access is through classes and performances, for example *Benched* on 30–31 October and 4–6 November 2026 at 18:00. There are no general sightseeing hours. The reception desk is staffed on weekdays 10–12.

sights.name: Søndermark Chapel and Crematorium
sights.blurb: A classicising chapel and crematorium with large and small halls and Einar Utzon-Frank's sculpture inside and out.
sights.when: The cemetery is always open. The urn hall is open 08–17 in October and 08–16 from November to February. The chapel halls (182 and 58 seats) are used for funerals, and there is no public interior access.

sights.name: Husumvold Church (Holger Jensen)
sights.blurb: A steep, stave-church-like roof on low yellow brick walls, with huge triangular gable windows, an atrium courtyard and a low bell tower.
sights.when: Active church.

sights.name: Sankt Nikolaj (Spreckelsen), Hvidovre
sights.blurb: A Catholic parish church from 1960.
sights.when: Active parish. Hvidovre is in the deprioritised south-west, but it is worth the detour. The address and opening hours are unverified.

sights.name: Vor Frue Catholic Church, Herlev
sights.blurb: Consecrated 1961; the parish was established in 1967. The architecture is undocumented in the sources consulted.
sights.when: Active. Treat it as a lead to scout.

sights.name: Herlev Hospital (Poul Gernes colours)
sights.blurb: A 25-storey, 120 m bed tower (one of Denmark's tallest buildings). It is joined to a fan-shaped concrete auditorium block and a four-storey treatment wing. Inside is Poul Gernes' complete polychrome scheme.
sights.when: Working hospital; the foyer is public during normal hours.
sights.q: Herlev Hospital, Borgmester Ib Juuls Vej 1, 2730 Herlev

sights.name: DTU Lyngby campus (Koppel grid)
sights.blurb: A rigid modular grid split into four quadrants by two axes. The standard buildings are in yellow brick with black window bands, and a forest belt was planted so the campus reads as "a town in a clearing".
sights.when: Open campus. Note that it is mostly brick, not concrete.
sights.q: DTU Building 101, Anker Engelunds Vej 1, 2800 Kongens Lyngby

sights.name: Kildeskovshallen pool (under renovation)
sights.blurb: Karen and Ebbe Clemmensen's listed sports and pool complex: swimming hall 1966–69, ball halls 1970–72, listed 1998, with a 2001 extension by Entasis.
sights.when: Renovation runs from 1 July 2026 to 2 January 2028. The 50 m pool and baby pool are closed, and Entrance A is closed until 2028. The 25 m, children's and diving pools stay open with changed hours.

sights.name: TV-Byen tower (old DR headquarters)
sights.blurb: A 15-storey office tower of concrete with aluminium and glass curtain walls; the remaining studio buildings have been converted into student housing.
sights.when: NCC is replacing the concrete and aluminium-and-glass façade for PensionDanmark, with completion expected in early 2027. The original skin is disappearing now.

sights.name: Fortunfortet
sights.blurb: A triangular fort sunk into the ridge, with only armoured turrets and domes showing above the glacis (the sloping earth bank in front).
sights.when: Casemates are normally locked; the outside can be reached from Fortunfortvej, Dyrehavegårdsvej or the Dyrehaven gate. It opens on Befæstningsdagen (last Sunday of September), so next opening is about September 2027.

sights.name: Lyngbyfortet
sights.blurb: A triangular sunken fort core, 172 m × 70 m, inside a villa road literally named Glaciset after the old earthwork. There are iron gates and shutters, and the moat is now a green.
sights.when: Closed except for Befæstningsdagen and occasional evening tours by Fæstningskanalens Venner. Time-sensitive context: a dispensation for a new house at Glaciset 47 was granted on 5 October 2026, with the appeal period running to 3 November 2026.

sights.name: Charlottenlund Fort and its howitzers
sights.blurb: A wet moat and bridge, the casemate building in the great traverse (the central earth-covered bank), the rangefinder entrance, and twelve 29 cm M/1910 howitzers still in their original positions.
sights.when: Grounds are open; there is a campsite and restaurant on site (hours not checked).

sights.name: Hvidøre Battery (private)
sights.blurb: A preserved ammunition magazine with "HVIDØRE" over the entrance, surrounded by houses. The previous owners added fake brick walls, an oak gate, a sentry box and Belgian cannons.
sights.when: Private; a local historian reports "Adgang for uvedkommende strengt forbudt" (no unauthorised entry). View from Rosavej only.

sights.name: Christiansholm Battery remains
sights.blurb: Only the throat (rear) front facing Hvidørevej survives.
sights.when: Viewable from the street.

sights.name: Taarbæk Fort (buried)
sights.blurb: A grassy elongated mound measuring 300 × 170 m.
sights.when: The mound is free to walk over; there is no interior access. A "buried ruin".

sights.name: Tinghøj Battery and the TV mast
sights.blurb: Built 1887–88 and complete in 1891. It is a protected monument, but the moat is partly filled in and built over, and the site has been used for hazardous storage and is partly contaminated.
sights.when: Private, and there is no access. A long-announced plan with the municipality to open it is unverified.

sights.name: Musikbunkeren (Cold War bunker)
sights.blurb: A civil-defence regional command bunker under Bernstorffsparken, now a youth music venue with about 14–15 rehearsal rooms, a studio and a 150-capacity concert room.
sights.when: Open 08–24 for users aged 15–25. The public can attend concerts. No heritage tours were found for 2026.

sights.name: WWII air-raid shelters, Gentofte
sights.blurb: One of 43 public WWII shelters built in Gentofte (111 were planned in May 1944). The Ericavej shelter by Kildebakke Station is the lead; most are sealed or reused.
sights.when: Mostly sealed or reused. Whether the Ericavej shelter still physically exists is unverified. These are good "found object" stops at most.

sights.name: Gunderød Nike site (ESK 531)
sights.blurb: A Nike air-defence battery for Copenhagen from 1959 to 1981, one of four (with Kongelunden, Sigerslev and Tune). It was taken off readiness first; the final Nike parade was held on 1 March 1983.
sights.when: A 2016 hiking account (not an official source) reports "adgang forbudt" and surviving remains. Current ownership and access are unverified. Do not confuse it with the separate radar station at Gunderødvej 33.

sights.name: Tinghøj Water Reservoir domes
sights.blurb: Two grass-covered plateaus over 10 underground reservoirs, totalling 10 ha.
sights.when: Fenced and not publicly accessible; view from Vandtårnsvej.

sights.name: Brønshøj Water Tower
sights.blurb: The report's lead was an Ib Lunding water tower at Bellahøj. The nearest match on the map is Brønshøj Water Tower, a raw concrete tower now used for concerts and exhibitions.
sights.when: Unverified: whether this is the tower the report meant, and its architect. Open for events; check the venue programme.

sights.name: Svanemølleværket power station
sights.blurb: A huge reinforced-concrete power station clad in red brick, visible across Nordhavn and Svanemøllebugten. Sources disagree on its size: By & Havn gives 21,000 m², Dansk Byudvikling 22,000 m² and Licitationen 26,000 m².
sights.when: Closed and handed to By & Havn (the city's port and development company).

p: This is the closest thing near Copenhagen to Gdańsk's Falowiec or Aillaud's estates: 24 blocks of three-storey offset terrace houses plus three blocks of shared facilities, clad in rusting corten steel. The rust gave the estate its nickname, 'Rustenborg'. Long internal access corridors run along the first floor, and underneath are vast column-and-beam parking decks.

It was built in 1970–75 by Fællestegnestuen (Jørn Ole Sørensen, Viggo Møller-Jensen and Tyge Arnfred) from 63,000 concrete elements. Bo Bedre called it 'Denmark's most advanced housing', and it won the Prix international d'Architecture in Brussels in 1973. The unit count differs by source: Trap Danmark gives 1,624, the housing association DOMINIA 1,645 and Fagbladet Boligen 1,580.

What makes it worth the trip is the scale of the idea: a whole town section of homes, paths and parking built as one system. A recent renovation repainted 19,000 m² of the access corridors, and the parking basements have been used as film locations.

Why it matters: it is one of Denmark's largest social housing estates and the purest local example of the 1970s megastructure. More than 4,000 people live here, so walk the public paths, keep cameras down near windows, and pair it with Flyvestation Værløse by bike.
farum.s: Trap Danmark/lex.dk; farum-midtpunkt.dk; arkitekturbilleder.dk; Fagbladet Boligen (2023); location from Google Places

p: Avedøre Stationsby is a total-planned town: a continuous ring of housing forms a 'town wall' with 'town gates', inspired by Dubrovnik. Inside are streets and a park, Byparken, with canals and bridges. At the S-train station stands Store Hus, a 464-flat slab whose split-level flats are served by lifts that stop only every third floor.

The town was built in 1972–82/84 to plans by Skaarup & Jespersen as AKB social housing for workers at Avedøre Holme, and it is in the Danish Architecture Centre's work register. Store Hus (1976–77, Ole Buhl) came late because of the 1973 building freeze. It was built for single middle managers, so the flats had kitchenettes and the building had a ground-floor restaurant.

Why it matters: with Farum Midtpunkt it is the strongest local answer to La Grande Borne, a whole town designed as one object. It is lived-in housing with public streets, and its services were renovated in 2020. Walk the wall and the park, and respect the residents.
avedore.s: Trap Danmark/lex.dk; Forstadsmuseet; arkitekturbilleder.dk; Paalsson Arkitekter; location from Google Places

p: Panum is a comb-shaped mass of concrete, brick and brown steel panels. Along Tagensvej a stepped wall carries sloped escape-stair balconies. It was built as a noise barrier for a planned urban motorway that was never built, so the building is defending itself against something that does not exist.

It was built from 1970/71 to 1986 by Eva & Nils Koppel, Gert Edstrand and Poul Erik Thyrring (KKET). Arkitekturbilleder.dk calls it one of Denmark's best-known examples of brutalist architecture, and the Danish Architecture Centre says it was clearly inspired by brutalism. Inside are board-marked concrete, colour-coded chimneys and stairs by Tonning Rasmussen, and Poul Gernes murals in the basement. The Mærsk Tower was added in 2017 and is now the main entrance.

Why it matters: it is the city's textbook brutalist building and still in full university use. The street perimeter is free to see. Access beyond the public foyer is not confirmed; Realdania By & Byg runs occasional guided visits. Google reviewers mention a free view lounge on the 15th floor of the Mærsk Tower, which I could not verify.
panum.s: Danish Architecture Centre; arkitekturbilleder.dk; da.wikipedia; Realdania By & Byg; location and view-lounge tip from Google Places reviews

p: This is a 30,000 m² walled prison of the panopticon era. On a tour you go through dungeons, security cells, isolation yards, the prison church and the workshops. The meeting point is Porten, the gate.

It opened in 1859 and was emptied of prisoners in 2015–16. In 2016–18 it held detained rejected asylum seekers, and in 2020 it was sold to PKA and A. Enggaard for redevelopment. It has been a film set for Olsen Banden, DR's *Huset* and *Underverden II*.

Tours are led by former staff. Porten runs them at weekends at 12:00 and 14:30 for 165 kr per adult (Vores Albertslund, September 2026). FOF had a tour on 20 October for 200 kr and AOF has one on 18 November for 190 kr. One organiser marketed its October tour as 'before it's too late', and it sold out.

Why it matters: it is the best legal way into a large abandoned institution near Copenhagen, and the window is closing. The redevelopment timeline is not confirmed, so book soon. Pair it with the Exners' Opstandelseskirken a short walk away.
vrids.s: vores-albertslund.dk; FOF; AOF; Liv i Sundby; en.wikipedia; location from Google Places

p: From outside it looks like a factory of glazed tiles and concrete, which is why it is nicknamed 'the grain silo'. Inside, a white in-situ concrete shell vault billows overhead like a cloud, lit from a hidden source. Lin Utzon designed the textiles.
Jørn Utzon designed it in 1968 and it was completed in 1976. It is in the Danish Culture Canon and widely regarded as a high point of European postwar church architecture.

Why it matters: this is the Danish concrete church to see if you see only one, and it is a short ride from Lyngby. Entry is free. It is open Tuesday to Friday 10–14 and on Sundays and holidays 12–16; Saturdays only from April to September, so not now. It closes on Mondays and during ceremonies, and the church recommends calling 48 hours ahead. Guided tours must be booked two weeks ahead.
bagsvaerd.s: bagsvaerdkirke.dk; sogn.dk; VisitCopenhagen; location from Google Places

p: In your own Lyngby there is a church of béton-brut walls and columns, with a freestanding concrete campanile, a concrete-slab forecourt, blue concrete-filled steel columns and a glass-block choir wall.

Carl R. Frederiksen built it in 1956–57 with engineer Ernst Ishøy. It is cited as Denmark's first pure concrete church. Kristeligt Dagblad describes it as a 'rectangular concrete box' in a style 'sometimes called brutalism'. Slots- og Kulturstyrelsen has listed it as a precursor of Bagsværd Church, despite the owner's reservations.

Why it matters: it is the beginning of the Danish concrete-church line that Bagsværd made famous, ten minutes from Mariebjerg cemetery. No general visiting hours are published, so go around Mass or contact the parish. Visitors mention an English Mass on Sundays at 12:00, which I could not verify.
knudlavard.s: Slots- og Kulturstyrelsen listing decision; Kristeligt Dagblad; kirkearkitektur.dk; arkitekturbilleder.dk; Mass tip from Google Places reviews

p: A slate-clad pyramid stands on a triangular plot, with an open bell chamber at its apex like a sea-mark. Inside, whitewashed exposed concrete rafters run up the corners.
Holger Jensen designed it, and it was consecrated in 1957, the same year as Sankt Knud Lavard.

Why it matters: Danish postwar churches are mostly brick, so the few with exposed concrete are worth finding. Hours are not published; Google lists weekday mornings, which I could not verify. The exterior alone is a two-minute stop.
lundehus.s: lex.dk; arkitekturbilleder.dk; location from Google Places

p: This is rough, irregular brick, not concrete. The nave is dark and cave-like and lit by skylights; the roof structure hangs about 4 m into the room, and you enter through a 'forest' of forged-iron columns. There is a corten water sculpture outside.
Inger and Johannes Exner built it in 1969–70. Kristeligt Dagblad calls it a main work of modern brick architecture.
Why it matters: it is the Exners' answer to the concrete churches, the same raw idea in brick. Hours are not published. It is a kilometre from the Ejbybunkeren on Vestvolden, so they pair well.
islev.s: lex.dk; arkitekturbilleder.dk; ingerogjohannesexner.dk; location from Google Places

p: A late church by Inger and Johannes Exner, from 1984, set in a landscape by Lea Nørgård.
The research found little more: there are some weekday services at 09:00. Google lists weekday daytime hours, which I could not verify, and it is probably shut at weekends, when the prison tours run.
Why it matters: it shows where the Exners went after Islev. Treat it as an exterior stop on the way to or from Vridsløselille.

About 25 hectares are laid out as a strict grid of square 'grave rooms'. Each room has its own planting, from clipped hedges to woodland burial and meadow, and a pollarded willow avenue runs through. The 1936 chapel and crematorium, in reinforced concrete, is by Frits Schlegel; the crematorium is now decommissioned.

G.N. Brandt planned it in 1926 and it was inaugurated on 6 October 1936. It is in the 2006 Danish Culture Canon, is regarded internationally as a main work of European garden art, and was shown at the 2014 Venice Biennale.

Why it matters: it is the closest Danish analogue to Auzelle's landscape cemeteries in Paris, and it is ten minutes from Sankt Knud Lavard. Open sunrise to sunset and free. Walk it room by room rather than along the main paths.
mariebjerg.s: lex.dk; Gentofte Kommune; Havehjernen; location from Google Places

p: A decorative-brick crematorium and chapel from 1960, with a copper entrance and a large skylight, in Nordre Kirkegård.
It is by Selchau, Brüel, Bornebusch and a young Henning Larsen. A new crematorium by Rytter Ark was reported under construction next to it; I could not verify whether it is finished.
Why it matters: it is a working example of designed death architecture in the suburbs, between the Vestvolden bunker and Vridsløselille. Visit quietly and keep away from ceremonies.
glostrup.s: arkitekturbilleder.dk; Rytter Ark; location from Google Places

ostra.t: Östra kyrkogården and Lewerentz's flower kiosk, Malmö
p: Malmö's largest cemetery holds Lewerentz's chapels of S:ta Gertrud, S:t Knut and Hoppets kapell, irrigation wells and urn graves. At the entrance stands his 1969 concrete flower kiosk: no gutters, and windows fixed with black mastic. Sveriges Radio calls it his 'most stripped-down and extreme' building, designed when he was over 80.
Lewerentz won the competition in 1917 with the entry 'Ås' and kept shaping the cemetery until 1969. He is buried here.
Form/Design Center has hosted a debate on returning the kiosk to its original role as the cemetery entrance, so its use may change.
Why it matters: this is the strongest reason to take a Skåne day, and the companion to Klippan's St Petri. The kiosk closes at 17:00, so start here or keep time for it.
ostra.s: Sveriges Radio; lewerentz.one; Skissernas Museum; Form/Design Center; location from Google Places

p: Inside is a single dark brick room, 18 × 18 m, held up by a central T-shaped iron cross. Lewerentz did not allow a single brick to be cut, so the mortar joints do all the adjusting. The font is a giant shell resting on a rock.
It was built in 1962–66 and consecrated in November 1966, and it draws architects from around the world.

Why it matters: it is brick rather than concrete, but it is the essential companion to Östra kyrkogården and one of the most radical rooms of the century. It is free and open every day, Monday to Friday 08–18 and weekends 10–18. Guided tours can be arranged by email.
klippan.s: sanktpetrikyrka.se; Svenska kyrkan Klippan; Riksantikvarieämbetet; location from Google Places

p: Trap Danmark describes a runway about 3 km long and 50 m wide, and you can walk, cycle or skate the whole of it. Around it are five 1930s hangars, Herkules hangars, 12 NATO hardened aircraft shelters, observation towers and heathland.

Danish Air Command was based here from 1951. Most of the base closed on 1 April 2004, it opened to the public in 2012, and Naturstyrelsen later removed the last thousand metres of fence. It is only about 20 km from Copenhagen's Town Hall Square.
Some shelters are rented out as storage (for example Shelter 333), and visitors mention a coffee stop at Shelter 214 (unverified). Hangar 46 (National Museum) has limited opening.

Why it matters: this is the closest thing near Copenhagen to a free-roam ruin, a Cold War landscape left open. Stay out of fenced areas such as the Freja and National Museum zones. Pair it with Farum Midtpunkt by bike.
vaerlose.s: Furesø Kommune; Ritzau/Naturstyrelsen; voresegedal.dk; hangar3.dk; Trap Danmark; coffee tip from Google Places reviews

p: Hangar 2 in the southern camp holds the Værløse Flyhistoriske Hangar, a collection of Danish Air Force aircraft and helicopters in various stages of restoration, run by volunteers.
It opens on Tuesdays 9–14 and Saturdays 13–16 with free entry; donations are welcome. Those hours come from a local listing, and Google shows the same.
Why it matters: it puts aircraft back into the airbase you have just walked. If you can only do one day, Tuesday or Saturday gives you both.
hangar2.s: hangar3.dk and local listings; Google Places

p: Inside the star-shaped citadel sits a German standard-type staff and command bunker, Regelbau 608. It was the last major structure built in Kastellet, intended as the Wehrmacht headquarters in case of an Allied landing.

During the Cold War it became the war headquarters of Military District Greater Copenhagen. Today it is a meeting place for Danmarks Veteraner and is open to all only on special days, according to Forsvaret.
Why it matters: it shows that the 17th-century citadel kept being a military site well into the nuclear age. The citadel is a free park, so the outside is always on the way.

A labyrinthine Cold War bunker is built into the 1880s Vestvolden rampart. It was the command bunker for Copenhagen's Nike air defence, and today it has interactive displays and a red artillery magazine with a café.

Self-guided visits run at weekends and in school holidays, 11–16, from the February to the October school break. It closes for self-guided visits after the autumn break; last year that was 20 October. Group tours run all year.
Prices differ: the official site gave 65/55/40 kr and KultuNaut 40/60 kr; treat the official figure as current.

Why it matters: it links the 1880s ring fortifications to the Nike missiles at Kongelunden. For late October 2026 check first whether it has already closed for the season. The rampart walk outside is free either way.
ejby.s: vestvolden.dk; Rødovre Kommune; KultuNaut; location from Google Places

p: A coastal fort from 1914–16 with radar platforms, a casemate, an observation bunker and a 1980s air-watch tower, with views over Køge Bay.
From 1959 to 1981 it was the radar and fire-control site for Nike squadron 532. To the north, three Nike magazine buildings survive on the common where the launch sites were.

Why it matters: it is a free, walkable Cold War site with no museum layer. Dragør Kommune runs it as an outdoor centre, open 08–20 every day. Visitors warn it sits under an airport take-off path, so expect the occasional jet.
kongelund.s: lex.dk; VisitDragør; koldkrig-online.dk; Amager Nyt (2020); location and jet tip from Google Places

p: North of Kongelundsfortet, three Nike magazine buildings survive on Kalvebod Fælled. The launch sites are visible on the common, and the munitions bunkers were reported open.
This was the firing area that the fort's radar controlled. The details come from a 2020 report in Amager Nyt, and the pin is rough, so look for the low buildings near Frieslandsvej.
Why it matters: this is one of the few places near Copenhagen where 'abandoned' really means abandoned. Do not confuse it with Sigerslev's private Nike site, which is off limits.
The largest fort of Copenhagen's 1880s land fortifications, near Jægersborg station. Inside are exhibitions designed with Experimentarium and a working 15 cm gun.

It opens at weekends and on holidays 10:30–16, and on school-holiday weekdays 11–15; adults pay 80 kr. The gun is fired on the last Sunday of each month at 12:00, which makes Sunday 25 October the date to aim for.
Why it matters: it is the most museumised of the ring forts and the closest to Lyngby. Combine it with Sankt Knud Lavard and Mariebjerg in one weekend morning.
garderhoj.s: garderhojfort.dk; Gentofte events; location from Google Places

p: An early fort of 1892–93, built with reinforced concrete. It is reportedly the only one of the ring forts with its storm railings intact, and it has an observation tower.
The grounds are free. The tower opens only on Fæstningsdagen, Fortification Day, in late September; that date comes from TripAdvisor.
Why it matters: it is a quick stop between Bagsværd Church and Farum, and an early use of reinforced concrete in Danish defence.
bagsfort.s: fredninger.dk; TripAdvisor; location from Google Places

p: An 1886–87 fort off Amager Strandvej, now a protected park. Visitors say the earthworks are larger than expected.
It was decommissioned in 1922 and closed by the Germans in 1940–47.
Why it matters: it is an easy stop on the Amager coast between Amagerbanen and Dragør. Daytime access is free; dogs must be on a lead and cycling inside is not allowed.
kastrup.s: lex.dk; grandts.dk; location from Google Places

p: A fort built in 1910–15 on a causeway south of Dragør harbour.

In the Second World War it was a German gunnery school, and later a coastal radar station until 2001. Today it is private, with a restaurant, hotel and events, and partial public access. Bringing your own food and drink is not allowed.
Why it matters: the walk out gives views of the water and the Øresund Bridge, and it pairs with Dragør's water posts in the old town.
dragorfort.s: VisitDragør; dragorfort.dk; location from Google Places

p: A First World War fort on the Køge Bay coast, now the museum Danmark 1914–18.
It opens Tuesday to Friday 11–15 and at weekends 11–16, and is closed on Mondays. Adults pay 110 kr and under-18s are free. A free introductory tour starts at 12:00.
Why it matters: it tells the story of a war Denmark stayed out of, from inside the defences built for it. Combine it with ARKEN and Avedøre on the same stretch of coast.
An artificial sea fort of 1890–94 in the Øresund, about 35 minutes by boat from Nyhavn. Havogkajak.dk calls it the world's largest sea fort; it cost 9.1 million kr at the time.
It was military until 1984. In 2015 Det Danske Spejderkorps, the Danish scout association, bought it with foundation support, and it now runs as a youth island.
Why it matters: it is the inner of the two great sea forts. Boats are seasonal, so this is one for the spring.
middelgrund.s: en.wikipedia; Spar Shipping; havogkajak.dk; location from Google Places

p: A sea fort of 1910–16, built on reinforced-concrete caissons cast at Lynetten and floated out into the Øresund, about 55 minutes by boat from Nyhavn.

It has been Swedish-owned (Malmökranen) since 2001. It was listed for sale on 29 January 2026 at 74.75 million kr (TV 2), and Euroman reported on 9 September that a new broker had cut the price to 42 million kr, which Yacht.de confirmed.

Why it matters: it may change hands before next season. Ferries ran from 25 April 2026, round-trip only and not on Mondays, and the restaurant usually runs to late September, so it is effectively closed now.
flak.s: TV 2; Euroman; Yacht.de; minbaad.dk; flakfortet.com; Spar Shipping; location from Google Places

p: Inside the chalk of Stevns Klint, a UNESCO site, run 1.7 km of tunnels 18 m deep. On the surface stand HAWK and Nike missiles.
The fort was built in 1950–53 to guard the southern Øresund and stayed in NATO service until 2000.

The underground fort can only be seen on guided tours of 24 people, booked through oesm.dk; the ticket includes all-day access to the grounds. Third-party hours conflict, so use the official site. A visitor reports there are no English tours and the app does not work underground (unverified).
Why it matters: it is the most complete Cold War installation in the region. It is outside Hovedstaden, about an hour's drive, so make it its own day.
stevns.s: oesm.dk; KultuNaut; location and tour tip from Google Places

p: In Krogenberg Hegn forest is Denmark's first nuclear-proof government bunker, built in 1958–61 under a concrete 'tortoise shell' and decorated inside by Poul Gernes.
It opened once, in 2013, and has been sealed since. All you can see is the fenced entrance in the forest.
Why it matters: only if you are passing. It adds a Cold War footnote to a North Zealand drive with the royal milestones.
gurre.s: BRS (2013); DR; location from Google Places

p: A hall 261 m long, up to 125 m wide and 27 m high: this is where the Øresund tunnel elements were cast in the 1990s, and it is one of Denmark's largest buildings. Inside are a free museum, the café Odds and Ends and the 3,000 m² TunnelArena.
The museum site lists Wednesday, Thursday and Friday, 10–14, for 2026; a Tuesday–Thursday line appears once, so Wednesday to Friday is the likely schedule.

Its future is in motion. The 2022 local plan allows about 400 homes inside, plus culture and offices. In April 2026 Nordhavn Avis reported the hall would be torn down and re-erected on a floor 3.4 m higher, and on 1 September Dansk Byudvikling reported that PensionDanmark is in advanced talks with By & Havn to develop the site.
Why it matters: it is the industrial cathedral of the bridge era, and it will not look like this much longer. Go on a weekday morning before the construction starts.
tunnel.s: museum.tunnelfabrikken.dk; Dansk Byudvikling; Nordhavn Avis; location from Google Places

p: The old shipyard island still has its 1960s section halls (used for Eurovision 2014), the old welding hall, the dry dock and the 'steel line' of connected production halls. The welding hall is now Copenhagen Contemporary, about 7,000 m² of art space.
Burmeister & Wain built ships here for 125 years, with up to 8,000 workers, until 1996. The area is designated a valuable cultural environment in the municipal plan.

Why it matters: it is the Copenhagen version of the Gdańsk shipyard, colonised by culture rather than left empty. It is free to wander, and the current mixed uses are assumed to continue until 2031, but masterplan proposals came out in May 2026, so redevelopment is coming.
refshale.s: Trap Danmark; Københavns Kommune KP24; refshaleoen.dk; Copenhagen Contemporary; location from Google Places

p: A limestone quarry 1,300 by 800 m and 65 m deep, one of northern Europe's largest open pits. It was worked from 1866 to 1994 and is kept dry by pumping.
In the words of Skönhetsrådet Malmö, the limestone became the Million Programme suburbs, so the hole is in a sense the negative of a lot of housing. It has been a nature reserve since 2010–11.

Why it matters: it is a legal ruin on a geological scale. The 4 km rim trail with viewpoints and binoculars is always open and free. The floor is guided-entry only because of landslide and quicksand risk; do not climb in.
limhamn.s: Länsstyrelsen Skåne; Udda Utflykter; en.wikipedia; location from Google Places

p: A green path follows the line of the inner freight railway from Lyngbyvej via Nørrebroparken and the Åbuen bridge to Valby: about 6 km on Frederiksberg and 2.5 km on Nørrebro.
The railway closed in 1930. Unlike the Petite Ceinture in Paris, it is fully landscaped, not wild. The route won Byplanprisen, the Danish urban planning prize, in 2013.
Why it matters: it is the city's rail trail, and the Åbuen arch is where you feel the old embankment. Use it as a car-free way to start the Nørrebro walk.
Along Uplandsgade a freight yard and track survive, and a cycle path along 'Ved Amagerbanen' follows the old line.

Passenger service ended in 1938 and the line closed in stages, fully by 1995. Since 2014 Amagerbanens Venner have run rail-bikes on about 500 m of track; visitors describe it as free and volunteer-run, and not open every day.
Why it matters: it is a small piece of abandoned railway inside the city. I could not verify the 2026 rail-bike dates, so treat a ride as a bonus.
amagerbanen.s: hovedstadshistorie.dk; Amagerbanens Venner; danskejernbaner.dk; location and visitor notes from Google Places

p: A cannonball is set into the brick facade next to the gateway, and on the facade toward Lindegården are two memorial tablets for the city fires of 1641 and 1728.

The University of Copenhagen's own history lexicon says the building, whose oldest part (the Munkekælderen cellar) is medieval, was damaged in the 1807 British bombardment 'but not more than could be repaired'. The same source describes the exact courtyard face slightly differently in two places, so look on both sides.
Why it matters: this is the best-documented of the walled-in cannonballs, Copenhagen's equivalent of the bullet holes in Athens. Start the Latin Quarter cannonball hunt here.
kommunitet.s: University of Copenhagen history lexicon; location from Google Places

p: Two doors along Nørregade carry walled-in shot: the Bispegården gate at number 11, and the gate at number 13.
The balls at number 13 are from the 1658–60 Swedish siege, not 1807; they were found during a 1900s rebuild and walled in. Sources disagree on 1659 versus 1807 for some balls in this cluster.
Why it matters: here two sieges a century and a half apart sit side by side, and both are on the facade.
norregade.s: Vandrefuglen; Politivennen Live Blogging; byvandring.milland.org; location from Google Places

p: Look up at first-floor height, behind a downpipe: a single iron ball set into the wall.

On 2–5 September 1807 the British fired thousands of shells and cannonballs and about 300 incendiary rockets on the city (figures vary: one walking-tour site gives 6,400 shells and 5,000 cannonballs; DR, citing historian Peter Henningsen, about 6,000 bombs and shells). The area from Vor Frue Kirke to today's Nørreport was devastated, and rebuilders walled in recovered shot 'so later generations would not forget'. Most balls did not land where they sit.
Why it matters: it is the easiest one to miss, which makes it a good test of the eye. Thirty seconds.
teglgard.s: Vandrefuglen; Politivennen Live Blogging; byvandring.milland.org; DR; location from Google Places

p: A cannonball sits above the gate of number 6.
The house dates from 1736 and survived the bombardment, so this is a pre-1807 building wearing a souvenir of it.
Why it matters: a quick look on the way between the Round Tower and the Workers' Museum.
gertrud.s: Vandrefuglen; Politivennen Live Blogging; location from Google Places

p: Go into the courtyard of number 7A and look at the rear building: a walled-in ball.
Courtyard access depends on the gate being open, often only in the daytime. The source list comes from local-history blogs, consistent with each other but not official.
Why it matters: it sits a few metres from the corner where the Golden Horns were melted, so you get two Pisserenden stories at once.
larsbjorn.s: Vandrefuglen; Politivennen Live Blogging; location from Google Places

krystal.t: Cannonball in the Main Library courtyard
p: In the courtyard of the Main Library a rear house survives, and left of its door a cannonball is set into the wall.
The usual story is that the ball hit right here. The Politivennen blogger who researched the cluster says that is almost certainly false: like most of these balls, it was found and walled in later.
Why it matters: it is the best place to see how a myth attaches to an object. The first Danish Stolpersteine are across the street.
krystal.s: Politivennen Live Blogging; Vandrefuglen; location from Google Places

p: At the corner of Vognmagergade and Landemærket, the former lighting-department headquarters (now KVUC, the adult-education centre) carries several cannonballs of different sizes.
It is part of the same 1807 cluster documented by local-history blogs.
Why it matters: the sizes vary, so you can see the range of shot used in the bombardment in one place.
kvuc.s: Vandrefuglen; Politivennen Live Blogging; location from Google Places

p: A couple of cannonballs are walled into the gateway of Jennows Gård.
Christianshavn was mostly out of range in 1807, but a few balls fell near here and were set into the gateway. That makes this the rare case where the shot plausibly landed close by.
Why it matters: it is the exception to the rule of the Latin Quarter balls. It rests on a single blog source, so treat it as unverified.
A cannonball sits above the entrance of number 8.
The local Østerbro walking-tour guide calls it an 'unknown cannonball' and says it is probably from 1807. Nobody has documented where it came from, and that is the story.
Why it matters: Østerbro was where the British siege lines ran, so a ball here makes sense, but nobody can prove it.
A plaque over a gate commemorates the Royal Life Jägers' part in the sortie at Classens Have, flanked by two walled-in cannonballs from the fight.

On 31 August 1807 Danish volunteer troops made a sortie against the British siege lines in Classens Have. Holsteinsgade is named after Major F.C. Holstein, who commanded the volunteer corps. It is one of the few sites tied to the land battle rather than the bombardment.
Why it matters: if you find it, it is the only marker of the 1807 fighting itself. The source is a privately produced guide and the building is not confirmed, so walk the street and look.

The royal house's own anniversary article says the bullet holes 'can still be seen today' in the palace masonry. Sources do not say exactly where, so look around the corners of Amaliegade, Frederiksgade and Ny Toldbodgade.

On the morning of 9 April 1940 the Royal Life Guards fought German infantry around Amalienborg while King Christian X, Prime Minister Stauning and the army chief met inside. Dengang.dk puts about 60 guardsmen in the fight and Livgardens Historiske Samling about 75; lex.dk confirms three were wounded. Fire ceased at 05:55 and Denmark capitulated at 06:00.
A Frihedsmuseet photo from the next day shows a police post at the Ny Toldbodgade corner with visible bullet holes, which is the best clue where to look.
Why it matters: it is the physical trace of the only fight in the capital on invasion day, inside a place you would otherwise skip as too famous.
amalienborg.s: kongehuset.dk; dengang.dk; Livgardens Historiske Samling; lex.dk; Frihedsmuseet

p: A 1950–51 office building stands on the exact site of the Gestapo headquarters, with a Danish memorial tablet and an RAF memorial tablet.

On 21 March 1945, in Operation Carthage, RAF Mosquitos destroyed the headquarters at rooftop height, and resistance prisoners held in the attic escaped. The rebuilt building was re-inaugurated on 30 June 1950.
Why it matters: it is the start of a two-part story whose second half, the French School, is 2 km west. Read the tablets here first.
shell.s: Dines Bogø (lokalhistorier.dk); airmen.dk; location from Google Places

p: A small memorial garden holds Max Andersen's 1953 granite sculpture of a mourning mother holding her dead child, in front of Ole Hagen's housing block on the school site. Visitors note paving stones along the path with the names of the dead.

In the first wave of the Shellhus raid one Mosquito hit a tall lamppost near the freight yard and crashed by the school, about 1.6 km from the target. Its smoke led seven or eight following aircraft to bomb Frederiksberg instead.

The death toll is reported inconsistently: 86 children and 18 adults (KultuNaut, Kristeligt Dagblad), 86 children and 19 adults (English Wikipedia), 106 at the school (Danish Wikipedia), and 124 Danes in total including 87 children (airmen.dk). The memorial was unveiled on 21 March 1953.
Why it matters: it is the other side of the Shellhus success, and the reason the raid is remembered with mixed feelings. Stand here after Shellhuset.
french.s: KultuNaut; Kristeligt Dagblad; Wikipedia (en, da); airmen.dk; location from Google Places

p: At the Henrettelsespladsen stand three bronze posts cast by the Lauritz Rasmussen foundry, exact copies of the German pine execution posts; the wooden originals went to Frihedsmuseet in 1967 because of wear. A plaque with Kaj Munk's lines 'Drenge, I drenge som døde…' marks where the German firing squad stood.

Elsewhere in the park are the Great Grave Field with 106 resistance burials and Axel Poulsen's mother-and-son sculpture, a rotunda for 31 concentration-camp dead, and a wall naming 151 whose remains were never found. The park was inaugurated on 5 May 1950.

Krigeren.dk reports 202 bodies found here after the war, 5 German soldiers and 197 Danish resistance fighters. How many were executed here varies by source: 94, 102 or 112. Park staff say the earliest executions took place at the nearby pistol range until summer 1944.

Why it matters: it is the most tangible execution site in the region. It is open daily (October 10–16, November and December 10–15), free, with free tours at weekends and on holidays. No dogs or bikes.
ryvangen.s: mindelunden.dk; krigeren.dk; copenhagenbykyhl.dk; Dines Bogø; airmen.dk; location from Google Places

p: On the rampart path is a cast concrete foundation of about 1 by 2 m with a rusting, overgrown central drain grate, built to carry away blood. There is no sign.

After the retroactive penal law of 1945, 78 death sentences were passed; 32 were commuted and 46 men were shot by volunteer police firing squads at night. Thirty were executed here and 16 at Undallslund near Viborg, from 1946 to 20 July 1950, and the shed was removed immediately after. Doctors pinned a paper target over each condemned man's heart.

Those shot here included the Brøndum gang, executed in seven volleys on the night of 8–9 May 1947, and Frikorps Danmark commander K.B. Martinsen on 25 June 1949. Historian Jes Fabricius Møller argues the site is 'theoretically listed but in practice unprotected', and gives 29 rather than 30.

Why it matters: it is the Danish state's own execution site, almost erased. The pin is approximate: look on the 2nd redan, nearest address Norddyssen 63. Christiania's no-photo rules apply around Pusher Street, which is elsewhere.
christiania.s: Jes Fabricius Møller; Kristeligt Dagblad; literature-based sources summarised in the research

gilleleje.t: Gilleleje church loft and October 1943 plaques
p: Round the town are bronze plaques by Gerda Thune Andersen, installed for the 75th anniversary, each telling the story of its spot: the station, the harbour auction quay, the old parish house and others. On Nordre Strandvej stands Karin Lind's split granite stone 'Forskudt Horisont' (2023), its upper half shifted sideways with 'Oktober 1943' cut into the ledge.

In early October 1943 between 500 and 600 Jews reached Gilleleje. When the harbour was sealed, refugees hid in lofts and in the church attic. On the night of 6–7 October an informer led Gestapo officer Hans Juhl to the church loft. The number taken varies by source, from about 50 to 86; Werner Best telegraphed Berlin that 110 Jews had been caught in Gilleleje. Many were sent to Theresienstadt.
The town then formed a committee and got about 500 more across. According to VisitNordsjælland, more than 7,000 Danish Jews reached Sweden that October.
Why it matters: it is the October 1943 rescue told street by street, including where it failed. Pair it with the Søren Kierkegaard path on the Gilleleje coast.
gilleleje.s: Museum Nordsjælland; VisitNordsjælland; folkedrab.dk; gillelejekirke.dk; POV International; location from Google Places

p: Cobble-sized stones with engraved brass plates give a name, birth year, date of deportation or flight, and fate. The three in front of the synagogue at Krystalgade 12 commemorate residents of the Meyers Minde home.

Gunter Demnig's project, the world's largest decentralised memorial, came to Denmark on 10 June 2019 with 12 stones. Copenhagen Municipality counted 53 by 2023, and 20 more were laid in the city in 2025. They commemorate deported Jews and communists, killed resistance fighters, police officers and victims of clearing murders.
Why it matters: once you have seen these you will notice others, for example at Nørregade 27, Nansensgade 19 and 52, Dyrkøb 3 and Heinesgade 1. They are always visible and free.
snublesten.s: Copenhagen Municipality decision document; lex.dk; snublesten.dk; location from Google Places

p: On the later Telephone building is an inscription and a relief of Ørsted holding a wire over a compass. The text reads, in Danish: in a house on this site the physicist Hans Christian Ørsted discovered electromagnetism in the year 1820.

Ørsted lived and taught at Nørregade 21 in 1819–24, when it housed the university's physics and chemistry rooms. During an evening lecture in spring (April) 1820, a current through a platinum wire deflected a compass needle in front of his students. He published in Latin on 21 July 1820.

Why it matters: it is an exact-spot 'first' of world importance. The original room is gone, so the inscription is the sight. The Niels Bohr Institute's physics walking route continues to Studiestræde 6, the later Polytechnic.
orsted.s: Niels Bohr Institute / University of Copenhagen page; location from Google Places

p: The old laboratory building stands at Gamle Carlsberg Vej, with the statue of founder J.C. Jacobsen in front; the laboratory buildings at numbers 6 and 10 are listed.

The laboratory was founded in 1875. S.P.L. Sørensen, head of the chemical department from 1901 to 1938, introduced pH in 'Enzymstudier II' in 1909. Emil Chr. Hansen's pure-culture lager yeast (1883) was also developed here, and in 2016 the lab re-brewed beer from yeast that had survived 133 years in an old bottle.
Why it matters: two pieces of everyday science started here. It is a working research centre, so the exterior is the sight; I found no dedicated pH plaque.
carlsberglab.s: Carlsberg history pages; lex.dk; location from Google Places
