p: In a woodland clearing near Kroppedal Museum, stones mark the walls and fireplace of a hut and the positions of the meridian-circle posts. A statue of Rømer, moved here in 1988 from the Technical University, stands nearby.

Rømer founded the observatory in 1704 with the world's first meridian circle; his earlier house observatory in Kannikestræde (1691) had the first transit instrument. It looked like a shack on purpose. The instruments went to the Round Tower in 1717, and most were lost in the 1728 fire.
Amateur archaeologist Claus Thykier, a music teacher, located the site in 1978 using calculations on sandwich paper.
Why it matters: it is a world first reduced to a few stones in a wood. Always open and free.
romer.s: UNESCO/IAU astronomical-heritage portal; lex.dk; location from Google Places

p: A small, ornate pavilion with a copper roof and a lantern, in a National Romantic style with Art Nouveau touches.

The kiosks of A/S Kjøbenhavns Telefonkiosker were staffed phone booths that also sold newspapers and stamps. According to grandts.dk this is the first one, put up on Kongens Nytorv on 1 June 1896 and later moved here. English Wikipedia gives 1896 for the first kiosks but 1 June 1906 for the opening of four, so the date is unresolved. Eight kiosks survive, most as cafés.
Why it matters: it is a piece of 1890s phone infrastructure still on the street. Google visitors say it now serves coffee, which fits the cafés the others became.
kiosk1.s: grandts.dk; en.wikipedia; location and current use from Google Places

kioskph.t: Listed telephone kiosk, Poul Henningsens Plads
p: A Fritz Koch telephone kiosk on Poul Henningsens Plads by Jagtvej.
It is the only one of his ten originals still in its original location. It was listed in 1994; Wikipedia gives both 1994 and 1996.
Why it matters: kiosk No. 1 was moved, this one never was. Its current use as a café is unverified.
kioskph.s: en.wikipedia (kiosk table); square location from Google Places

p: By the Court House on Nytorv stand a 1913 kiosk of the Jensen model, still in its place, and a dark-green, fully screened cast-iron pissoir.

According to Information (2016), the city's first pissoirs of 1888, nicknamed 'De Ehlerske Mavebælter' (Ehlers' belly-belts), screened only the essentials. Complaints made the city pay for the fuller green type, which 'can still be seen (and smelled)' here and on Nikolaj Plads.

Background: a paid women's toilet at Nikolaj Kirke from 1886, the first municipally funded public toilet in 1902, and underground toilets for both sexes at Amagertorv in 1902. Copenhagen only got sewers from about 1860 and was allowed to connect flush toilets in 1894; Nakskov was first in 1884.
Why it matters: it is the closest Copenhagen comes to the Paris vespasienne. The pissoir's 2026 state rests on a 2016 article, so confirm on site.
nytorv.s: Information (2016); en.wikipedia kiosk table; square location from Google Places

p: A dark-green, fully screened cast-iron urinal on Nikolaj Plads, the twin of the one on Nytorv.
The square also had Copenhagen's paid women's toilet at Nikolaj Kirke from 1886.
Why it matters: two minutes, and it sits outside Nikolaj Kunsthal's sound-art show in the old church. Confirm it is still there; the source is from 2016.
nikpissoir.s: Information (2016); square location from Google Places

p: A kiosk of the 1913 model on Kongens Nytorv. It was moved a few metres when the square was refurbished in 2004.
Kiosk No. 1 started here in 1896 (or 1906) before it was moved to Christianshavn.
Why it matters: it is a ten-second stop between Hviids Vinstue and the McDonald's that replaced Kierkegaard's café.
A Fritz Koch telephone kiosk, moved to Dyrehavsbakken from the corner of Store Kongensgade and Gernersgade, stands at Dyrehavevej 62.
Bakken opens seasonally, and I could not confirm the kiosk's current state.
Why it matters: it is the nearest kiosk to Lyngby and an easy add-on to the Bakken and Ordrupgaard area.

lyngbyvej.t: Royal milestone on Lyngbyvej ('FV ¾ M')
p: A protected red-granite stone of about 30 by 30 by 70 cm, marked 'FV ¾ M': three-quarters of a Danish mile from the city gate, under Frederik V's monogram.

The chaussée reforms of the 1770s–90s put marble obelisks at every full and half Danish mile (about 7.5 km) and hewn fieldstones at the quarters. Frost destroyed the marble, so Christian VIII replaced many in Bornholm granite, and a rescript of 1842 ordered the original king's cipher re-cut. That is why stones carry Frederik V's monogram decades after his death.
Why it matters: it turns a motorway verge into an 18th-century road. The exact spot is not confirmed and the stone has likely been moved, so look before relying on the pin.
lyngbyvej.s: Slots- og Kulturstyrelsen, Fund og Fortidsminder

p: On Hørsholm's pedestrian street, by the optician at number 24, stands a stone marked 'FV 3¼ M', repainted by the local museum society.
Distances were counted from Copenhagen's old city gates along the King's Road network.
Why it matters: it is the easiest of the milestones to find, and the first stop on a North Zealand drive.
horsholm.s: Ugebladet Hørsholm; location from Google Places

nyrup.t: Royal milestone and King's Road, Nyrup Hegn
p: In front of Naturcenter Nyruphus at Ferdinandshøj stands a 5½-mile obelisk of Norwegian marble with a posthorn and Christian VII's monogram.
In Nyrup Hegn you can also walk stretches of Frederik II's private paved King's Road of 1584.
Why it matters: this is the best preserved of the milestones, and the old road surface is still underfoot.
nyrup.s: Helsingør Leksikon; location from Google Places

p: Two public water posts survive in Dragør's cobbled old town, on Hans Isbrandtsens Plads and Jens Eyberts Plads.
Before the 1907 waterworks the town relied on wells and nine public street posts; only these two are left. The source is a single local-history site.
Why it matters: no historic street water post was confirmed inside Copenhagen, so this is the substitute, and Dragør's old town is worth the walk.
An 1859 yellow-brick engine house by N.S. Nebelong, with round-arched cast-iron windows.

It was Denmark's first waterworks and one of the first buildings outside the old walls, and it ran until 1951. It is a rare early use of cast-iron columns and decks in Denmark, became an industrial heritage site in 2007 and was listed in 2010.
Why it matters: it is the answer to the cholera of 1853 that hit the next stop, Pisserenden. Today it is a concert venue, so you only get inside for a gig.
pumpehuset.s: Slots- og Kulturstyrelsen listing; location from Google Places

goldhorns.t: Where the Golden Horns were melted
p: There is nothing to see: this is just a corner in the medieval street grid. The story is the sight.

In a kitchen on this corner the goldsmith and forger Niels Heidenreich hacked up and melted the stolen Golden Horns of Gallehus, a national treasure lost for good. The district nickname Pisserenden ('the piss gutter') comes from the open gutters that carried urine and waste before sewers; the area was hit hard by the 1853 cholera, which triggered Copenhagen's sanitary reforms.
Why it matters: it is a 'spot without a trace' with a good story. The exact building is not documented, so treat it as this corner.
An 18th-century sheer-leg crane building in timber and brick faces the harbour from Nyholm. It was used to step masts into warships.
Philip de Lange designed it and it was built in 1748–51; it was fitted out as a museum in 1994.

Access is the weak point: Nyholm is a naval area reported open to the public, and Google visitors say that if you ask at the ticket office a guide unlocks the gates and takes you up for one of the best views of the city. None of that is verified, so treat it as a view-from-across stop that might turn into more.
mastekran.s: TripAdvisor and cruise blog (access); Google Places reviews (climb tip)

p: On the island of Ven you can see Stjerneborg, Tycho Brahe's partly reconstructed underground observatory (excavated in the 1950s, opened in 2002), the marked footprint of Uraniborg with recreated Renaissance gardens, and in St Ibb's church Tycho's own pew with the Brahe crest and an altarpiece he commissioned.

Frederik II gave Tycho the island in 1576, and his observations let Kepler derive his laws. In 1671 Rømer and Picard measured the longitude difference between Paris, the Round Tower and Uraniborg here.

Why it matters: it is the origin of the Rømer story at Tusculanum. The museum is open daily from May to August and on September weekends, so it is closed now; visitors also complain the observatory costs extra.
ven.s: sydsverige.dk; location and fee complaint from Google Places reviews

p: Left of the cathedral's main entrance is an automaton clock. Two knights clash swords on the hour, and at the scheduled plays the Three Magi process past Mary and the Child while a small organ plays 'In dulci jubilo'. The calendar disc runs from 1923 to 2123.

Dendrochronology dates it to about 1422–25, probably by Nicolaus Lilienfeld of Rostock. It was dismantled in 1837, reconstructed in 1923 after 15 years of research by Theodor Wåhlin and the Danish clockmaker Julius Bertram-Larsen, and restored again in 2010 by the Danish clockmaker Søren Andersen. It has been in Sweden's cultural canon since 2025.

Why it matters: it is a working 600-year-old machine, and a Danish craft story as much as a Swedish one. Time the visit: Monday to Saturday 12:00 and 15:00, Sunday 13:00 and 15:00, with a short talk at 11:45 on weekdays and Saturdays. Entry to the cathedral is free.
lundclock.s: Svenska kyrkan (official); location from Google Places

p: A working reading room inside the 1906 library building, entered through the Black Diamond, with Johannes Magdahl-Nielsen's green glass desk lamps.

The library names Georg Brandes and Lenin among its famous users and says Lenin had a permanent seat, chair number 9, when he stayed in Copenhagen in 1910. Carl Thomsen's 1970 Royal Library pamphlet draws on a taped account by a reader who worked at the same table, and cites a reading-room receipt for 'Ulianof' dated 15 September 1910, after the socialist congress had ended. Lenin lodged in a back room at Vesterbrogade 112A and is said to have walked here daily to read Danish agricultural and cooperative statistics.
Two cautions: I found no primary document for the 'chair 9' detail, which comes from library lore and the University Post; and Kierkegaard died in 1855 and never used this building.

Why it matters: it is the closest Copenhagen comes to the Brussels café where Marx worked, a revolutionary's named seat in a room still used for reading. Non-students can sit at length on the free Læsesalon evenings, 11 November and 9 December at 16:30. A third-party guide says the room can be entered on Sundays with an exhibition ticket; check with the library.
laesesal.s: Det Kgl. Bibliotek; Carl Thomsen, 'Lenin's visits to Denmark' (1970); University Post; swedishtraveler.com; location from Google Places

p: The original lecture hall of 1921 is still in use, and Bohr's office has been kept intact.

The institute opened in 1921 as Bohr's Institute for Theoretical Physics. Its head describes Auditorium A as the place 'where Niels Bohr and his allies worked and argued', which covers the Copenhagen-interpretation era and visitors such as Heisenberg, Pauli, Dirac and Gamow.

Most of the institute moved to the new Niels Bohr Building on Jagtvej in 2024; the historic buildings remain. The Niels Bohr Archive says no public historical tours are offered until further notice because of renovation. The realistic way in is the Niels Bohr International Academy's annual public lecture series with Folkeuniversitet, held in Auditorium A. The institute used to hold an open day every February.
Why it matters: it is a 'same room, same use' site of modern physics. From outside it is a short stop next to Panum; inside, watch the Folkeuniversitet programme.
bohr.s: Niels Bohr Archive; Niels Bohr Institute; Folkeuniversitet i København; location from Google Places

p: A dark cellar wine bar of several rooms, serving smørrebrød at lunch and gløgg in winter.

It was founded in 1723, calls itself the oldest wine bar in Copenhagen, and still occupies the same rooms. Its own history says it has had many artists and intellectuals as regulars without naming any, and an Andersen-fan site says many actors from the Royal Theatre across the square drank here.

Myth flag: there is an H.C. Andersen medallion at the side entrance, but even the fan site says whether he was ever there 'is not known', and a VoiceMap Andersen tour says there is no record of him here.
Why it matters: it is an authentic room with three centuries of the Golden Age theatre milieu, not Andersen's bar. Open daily; just walk in.
hviids.s: Hviids Vinstue history page; Andersen-fan site; VoiceMap; location from Google Places

p: The rear building at Rømersgade 22 was built in 1879 as the labour movement's assembly house, with a banquet hall and meeting rooms. The museum calls it the oldest workers' assembly building in Europe, and it is on the shortlist for nomination as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The festsal was restored to its 1913 look and had a major restoration in 2021.
In the basement is Copenhagen's only listed basement tavern, restored to its 1892 appearance and run under its original name. You can eat smørrebrød and drink beer in the actual room.

Social-Demokraten had its editorial office on the ground floor for 21 years, and Thorvald Stauning had an office here; the museum shows objects from it. Secondary sources say Lenin, Rosa Luxemburg and Clara Zetkin visited or spoke here in 1910, which is plausible but secondhand. A claim that Louis Pio spoke here is wrong: he emigrated in 1877, before the building opened.

Why it matters: it is one of the two strongest still-operating rooms in the city. The museum is open daily 10–17 (Thursday to 20); the Øl-Halle's listed hours differ, so check. Lenin's statue is inside the museum.
arbejder.s: Arbejdermuseet; Parkmuseerne; location from Google Places

p: A traditional Danish lunch and dinner restaurant in low cellar rooms hung with old paintings.
The restaurant says it dates from 1720 and that Andersen came every day in 1854 while writing The Ugly Duckling; it also claims Kierkegaard.

Reality check: the present building was built in 1828–29 by master mason Christian Olsen Aagaard on an earlier fire site; the restaurant traded as 'Peter Fabers Minde' in the early 1930s and took its present name around 1940; and The Ugly Duckling was published in 1843. Even friendly guides call the story legend.
Why it matters: it is a lovely old room with marketing-grade thinker claims, a good lesson in how these stories are made.
apotek.s: Det Lille Apotek homepage; indenforvoldene.dk; location from Google Places

p: A tiny red-walled bodega, open since 1917, smoky, with décor described as unchanged.

It sits opposite the Gyldendal publishing house, and VisitCopenhagen says artists, officials, journalists and office workers have hung out here since the First World War. It was a location in Christian Braad Thomsen's film The Blue Monk (1998).
No named author is documented as a regular, and the story that a sailor bought the first bar counter in Copenhagen is presented even by VisitCopenhagen as legend.
Why it matters: it is a living room of the publishing quarter. Smoking is allowed inside, so decide before you go in.
A Parisian-style café and bar that opened in 1977, with covers of Turèll's books along the bar and a jukebox.
Turèll was a regular. The house story is that he gave the café his name in exchange for free food and drink; even the tourist board says 'legend has it'.
Why it matters: it is the 1970s bohemian layer of the city, though a recent renovation into a partly cocktail and wine bar has overwritten some of it.

josty.t: House of Josty, Frederiksberg Gardens (Kierkegaard's café)
p: A public café facing Frederiksberg Gardens, with a B&B and event rooms.

Kierkegaard's pseudonym Johannes Climacus writes in Concluding Unscientific Postscript: 'As usual, I was sitting outside the café in Frederiksberg Gardens… There as usual I sat and smoked my cigar.' This is the scene where he decides to become an author who makes things harder, and his journal repeats it. Identifying 'the café' as Josty is the standard reading, not something the text says.

Josty got its licence in 1824 and built a pavilion that Copenhagen Museum says was used without major changes until 1899, when it was torn down for a larger restaurant. So you sit on the same site, in the same business, but not in Kierkegaard's building.
Why it matters: it is Kierkegaard's best surviving spot. It reopened in 2026 under new management as House of Josty: Tuesday to Friday 8–17, weekends 9–17, kitchen until 15:00.
josty.s: Kierkegaard, Concluding Unscientific Postscript and journals; Copenhagen Museum; houseofjosty.com; location from Google Places

p: Halfway up the spiral ramp is the Library Hall, now an exhibition and concert hall with modern fittings.

This was the University Library from 1657 to 1861 (rebuilt after the fire of 1728). The Round Tower says the young H.C. Andersen was allowed to use its books 'provided that he put the books properly away after use'. Students of Kierkegaard's day reached it by the ramp, and the Stone–Bronze–Iron Age system was first formulated here while the antiquities collection was being arranged.
Why it matters: same room, different use. The tower ticket includes it, and the observatory on top was used by the university from 1642 to 1861.
J.D. Herholdt's cast-iron book hall of 1861 is still full of books on two levels.

It was the Latin Quarter's university library until 2009, and it came out of Denmark's first public architectural competition, held in 1855. It reopened to the public on 3 October 2023 'not as a library, not as a museum'.

Why it matters: my sources name no specific users, so it is atmosphere rather than 'X sat here', but you can still walk among and open the books. The 2023 hours were Tuesday–Wednesday and Friday–Saturday 10–16 and Thursday 10–20, at 75 kr, with daily tours at 13:00 in Danish and 14:00 in English; Google now lists slightly different times, so check.
fiol.s: University of Copenhagen; location and current listing from Google Places

p: A student college since 1623, opposite the Round Tower, with a courtyard and a linden tree.

The first linden was planted on 12 May 1785 'as a gathering point for the students' parties and discussions', and Studenterforeningen was founded at a party in the Regensen garden on 16 July 1820. The original tree died in 1953; the current one is a replacement, and Regensen's own timeline and Uniavisen tell different versions of how it was lost.

Why it matters: it is a living student institution. It is a private residence, so you glimpse it through the gate except on Culture Night, at flea markets or on a booked tour. Regensen's Linden Ball hangs lanterns in the tree.
regensen.s: Regensen timeline; Uniavisen; location from Google Places

p: The university's main building on Frue Plads, still in daily use.

On 3 November 1871 Georg Brandes gave his first lecture of Hovedstrømninger (Main Currents) 'in auditorium 7 on Frue Plads', which began the Modern Breakthrough in Scandinavian literature. The university held its 150th-anniversary seminar in Festsalen, 'where it all started'.
Why it matters: it is a lecture hall you can still enter for a public lecture or event. There is no exhibit, so check the university's events.
frueplads.s: University of Copenhagen; location from Google Places

p: A palace on Bredgade, now a private event and concert venue.

The 8th International Socialist Congress met here on 28 August–3 September 1910, with 896 delegates from 23 countries according to the Marxists Internet Archive (a contemporary observer counted 887). Stauning's Social Democrats hosted. Lenin, Rosa Luxemburg and Jean Jaurès attended, and Plekhanov, Zinoviev, Kamenev and Trotsky are also named.
Why it matters: it is where Lenin's Copenhagen stay began. You only get in for a concert or event, so it pairs with the Royal Library reading room he walked to.
oddfellow.s: Marxists Internet Archive; International Socialist Review (Emil Stultz); location from Google Places

p: A student café, bar and meeting place next to the Round Tower.

A plaque records that Studenterforeningen had its first rooms here from November 1820 to 1824. The association lists Oehlenschläger, Andersen, Kierkegaard and Thorvaldsen among those who came to it, though not necessarily to this building.
Why it matters: the same kind of use continues, and it is the cheapest seat on the thinkers' list.
studenterhuset.s: Studenterforeningen history; location from Google Places

p: A free botanical garden on the edge of central Lund.

Strindberg lived in Lund from December 1896 to August 1897 and from April 1898 to 20 June 1899, writing Inferno, To Damascus I–II and Gustav Vasa. Lund's tourist office describes his rigid routine: a morning walk, often here or along Södra Vallpromenaden, then lunch and dinner at the inn Åke Hans with coffee, billiards and punsch among radical students until 23:00. Only the street front of Åke Hans survives, and it is no longer an inn.

Why it matters: the ground is authentic even if the seat is not. Lund's tourist office publishes a two-hour Strindberg walk. Visitors report the greenhouse, café and toilets are closed for renovation until 2027.
lundbot.s: Lund tourist office; location and renovation note from Google Places reviews

p: A quiet garden behind Christiansborg, between the old library and Rigsarkivet, with a reflecting pool and Louis Hasselriis' statue of Kierkegaard, said to gaze toward where Regine Olsen lived.
The garden dates from after the 1906 library, so Kierkegaard never sat here.
Why it matters: it is a good bench before or after the reading room next door.
kblhave.s: Det Kgl. Bibliotek; location from Google Places

p: Nørrebro locals use the cemetery as a park, and its benches are a long-standing reading spot.
The graves of Søren Kierkegaard, H.C. Andersen and Niels Bohr are here. Visitors note that many famous headstones are modern replacements.

Why it matters: it is a grave-and-garden visit, not 'where they sat', but it ties the thinkers' list together. On Sunday 25 October at 14:00 Christian Kronman gives the last of his Sunday cemetery tours. LiteraturHaus is across Møllegade.
assistens.s: Research report 3 and 4; location and headstone note from Google Places

p: A McDonald's on Kongens Nytorv, in a building of 1857.

This was a konditori from 1792, known as Mini's in Kierkegaard's and Andersen's time. In 1857 Stephan à Porta tore down the previous house and built a new one, so the room they knew is gone. Café à Porta, with a fake-1850s interior from 1999, went bankrupt in 2011/12 and has been a McDonald's since. A German-language source says Mini's and Pleisch were the two ends of the dandies' afternoon route and that Kierkegaard read newspapers and drank punch at Pleisch, which is also gone.
Why it matters: it is the perfect rejected entry, a reminder that most 'Kierkegaard cafés' are stories, not rooms.
aporta.s: Research report 3 (rejected list); location from Google Places
u: A Porta - Wikipedia, den frie encyklopædi

p: A house on Vesterbrogade with a plaque for Lenin, hidden in a locked back courtyard.
Lenin rented 'a backroom, 112 Vesterbrogade' (Carl Thomsen's pamphlet) during his 1910 stay, from where he is said to have walked daily to the Royal Library reading room.
Why it matters: it is excluded from the thinkers' list as a house, but it is a 30-second pass-by on the way from Shellhuset to the French School.
lenin.s: Carl Thomsen, 'Lenin's visits to Denmark' (1970); research report 3; location from Google Places
u: Lenin in Copenhagen - Swedish traveler exploring Copenhagen

p: Bertel Thorvaldsen is buried in the open courtyard of his museum, among Egyptian-style paintings of palms, lions and crocodiles. The museum, opened in 1848, was Denmark's first public museum building.

In August 2026 the museum announced 9 million kr from A.P. Møller Fonden, matched by Copenhagen Municipality (18 million kr in total), for the first major work on the courtyard facades in more than 80 years. Migogkbh.dk reports the courtyard will be closed to the public during the 2026–27 restoration, so the grave may not be viewable.
Why it matters: it is a grave inside an art museum. Entry is free on Wednesdays and the museum is closed on Mondays; its own painting collection is on show (see Events).
thorvaldsen.s: Thorvaldsens Museum; migogkbh.dk; location from Google Places
u: Thorvaldsens Museum åbner dørene til en mindre kendt del af guldalderen med ny udstilling

p: A wooden exhibition building of 1893 designed by J.F. Willumsen, with a gilded Pegasus over the door.
It was moved to Oslo Plads in 1898 and is one of the first Danish buildings designed specifically for art exhibitions.
Why it matters: a moved wooden 'temple' is an oddity in itself. Toaster's Nervetråde show ends on 1 November, with a performance night on 22 October; the building then closes until 7 November.
denfrie.s: Research report 4; location from Google Places

p: A former DSB locomotive workshop at Otto Busses Vej, now used for fairs and events; Kunst for Alle was held here on 2–4 October.
The research logged it as an industrial reuse and found no more detail.
Why it matters: it is a big railway hall on the edge of the Carlsberg and Sydhavn area. You only get inside for an event.
lokomotiv.s: Research report 4; location from Google Places

p: Denmark's largest cemetery, a designed landscape in the south-west of the city. The pin is its Nordre Kapel.

On Saturday 31 October, 14–17, the chapel hosts 'De Dødes Dag': light a candle, write a letter, tie a spruce bouquet or plant a bulb; a talk on grief by Anne Hjernøe at 15:00; and at 16:00 the names of the dead are read aloud. Coffee and cake; it appears to be free.
Why it matters: it adds a third designed cemetery to Mariebjerg and Assistens, and the 31 October afternoon is the best All Saints happening in the window.
vestre.s: Research report 4; location from Google Places

p: A ship-shaped concrete museum of 1996 by Søren Robert Lund, set on the beach park of Køge Bay.
SUPERFLEX's current show turns it into a 'sunken ark' (see Events).
Why it matters: it is one of the few concrete landmarks of the 1990s here, and it sits between Avedøre and Mosede on the coast.
arken.s: Research report 4; location from Google Places
u: Calendar | ARKEN Museum of Contemporary Art

p: An art museum north of the city with a concrete extension by Zaha Hadid and the architect Finn Juhl's own house in the art park.
From 23 October (24 in one listing) the cabinetmakers' annual experimental furniture show fills the museum, Finn Juhl's House and the park, about light and form.
Why it matters: Hadid's concrete is the reason it is on this map, and it is 15 minutes from Lyngby.
ordrupgaard.s: Research report 4; sn.dk; location from Google Places

p: The museum is housed in John Smedberg's 1901 power station, with Tham & Videgård's perforated orange extension.
On Friday 23 October at 17:00 it opens Anu Põder and Anna Casparsson (see Events).
Why it matters: industrial reuse with a strong modern addition, on the Malmö day between the quarry and Lewerentz.
modmalmo.s: Research report 4; location from Google Places

p: 28 free-standing point towers of 9–13 storeys on the Bellahøj ridge. They are paired around glass stair and lift towers, with patterned tile cladding that varies between the four builders, and sit in open parkland with underground garages.

Tage Nielsen and Mogens Irming won the 1944 competition. The towers were built 1950–57 by four social housing companies, each with its own architect (including Eske Kristensen, Edvard Heiberg and Dan Fink). Construction used reinforced concrete, prefabricated elements and slipforming, first tested on a prototype building in Herlev. They are Denmark's first high-rises, and the Le Corbusier influence is direct.

In 2021 serious construction errors were found in the ten towers owned by SAB; in strong wind there is a risk of collapse. Renovation was ruled out on cost: Licitationen reports that a DKK 436 million price rise pushed the total for SAB's 10 towers (487 homes) to DKK 2.6 billion. The Borgerrepræsentationen (Copenhagen City Council) started a local plan for demolition and rebuilding in March 2026. On 22 June 2026 a committee majority allowed SAB to strip the three empty Bellahøj Syd towers. According to the residents' site bellahoj.com, contractor SØNDERGAARD set up the site in week 39 and began stripping in week 40, with a work plan running to week 20 of 2027. Akademiraadet (the Royal Academy's arts council) objected on 22 June. The other 18 towers are not affected. The grounds are public; the buildings are private homes.
bellahoj.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 1); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

p: Five 16-storey and two 9-storey slab blocks lined up as a wall on the hilltop above Utterslev Mose. The north side has deck-access walkways; the park side has the blue façades from the 1990s.

Built 1962–68 by Hoff & Windinge with Jørgen Juul Møller, Kai Agertoft and Alex Poulsen. According to Magasinet Beton (DI), its 1,943 homes housed about 7,000 residents. It is described as Denmark's first large montage (prefabricated) building project. Cars and pedestrians are fully separated. A park of about 500,000 m² was set aside and protected under a 1969 declaration. A5 Tegnestuen renovated the estate in 1991–93.
Lived in, and the park is open. The north decks are best seen from the car parks.
hojegladsaxe.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 2); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

p: A yellow-brick "new town" of three-storey blocks. Its landmark is a 13-storey tower visible from Grundtvigs Kirke across Utterslev Mose. There are landscape spaces by C.Th. Sørensen.

Planned from 1950 by Steen Eiler Rasmussen (who also made the Fingerplan, Copenhagen's 1947 regional plan) and built 1950–71 on English new-town ideals. It is brick, not concrete, but it is the essential counterpoint to Bellahøj.

The Borgerrepræsentationen voted to demolish Steen Eiler Rasmussen's 42 Langhusvej rowhouses from 1970 and removed their preservation status, as part of the plan required by the parallel-societies law. Check whether they are still standing before you go.
tingbjerg.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 3); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

p: Brick slab blocks from just after the war, with star patterns cast into the concrete balconies.
Built 1948 by Svenn Eske Kristensen, and singled out by Trap Danmark for its balcony decoration.
Lived in and public from the street. The exact address and coordinates are unverified.
herlevvaenge.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 4); pin from the report, approximate.

p: Restrained red brick on the outside, a free-standing concrete bell tower with an open bell chamber and cross motifs between the two wings, and inside a bright concrete space with a flat barrel vault.

The parish wing dates from 1923–24 (Julius Smith). The church hall was finished in 1960 by Richard Jessen. Frank Maali and Gemma Lalanda renovated it in 2018, and the black metal-and-glass furnishings are by Maali. Lex describes the contrast between plain exterior and concrete interior as the point of the building.
Active parish church; the interior is open during services or opening hours, which were not checked.
enghave.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 5); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

p: A strictly symmetrical plan from 1903 that has softened into parkland. Its poplar avenue continues the axis of Grundtvigs Kirke down to Utterslev Mose. There is a cherry avenue, the columbarium, and the Friis & Moltke crematorium of 2001–03 on the site of the demolished Østre Kapel.

A crematorium has stood here since 1908. The current one is Denmark's largest; Copenhagen's Teknik- og Miljøudvalget (technical and environment committee) said on 15 December 2025 that it carries out about 5,200 cremations a year. The cemetery contains Denmark's largest communal grave, holding up to about 100,000 ashes.
Open, free.
bispebjerg.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 6); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

p: A domed crematorium building from the early 1900s, converted into a municipal dance house.

Designed by Holger Jacobsen (1876–1960) for Foreningen for Ligbrænding (the cremation society), which had earlier run the Nyelandsvej crematorium on Frederiksberg. The 1908 date comes from secondary sources.

An active Københavns Kommune venue. Access is through classes and performances, for example *Benched* on 30–31 October and 4–6 November 2026 at 18:00. There are no general sightseeing hours. The reception desk is staffed on weekdays 10–12.
dansekapellet.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 7); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

p: A classicising chapel and crematorium with large and small halls and Einar Utzon-Frank's sculpture inside and out.
By Frits Schlegel and Edvard Thomsen, built 1927–29 (often dated 1928). It predates Schlegel's concrete masterpiece at Mariebjerg, so it is useful to see the two together.

The cemetery is always open. The urn hall is open 08–17 in October and 08–16 from November to February. The chapel halls (182 and 58 seats) are used for funerals, and there is no public interior access.
sondermark.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 8); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

p: A steep, stave-church-like roof on low yellow brick walls, with huge triangular gable windows, an atrium courtyard and a low bell tower.

Holger Jensen, 1960. It replaced a temporary barrack church on the old fortification rampart. It is brick and timber rather than concrete. Include it mainly as part of a Holger Jensen series alongside the already-covered Lundehus Kirke.
Active church.
husumvold.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 9); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

p: A Catholic parish church from 1960.

Designed by Johan Otto von Spreckelsen (later the architect of the Grande Arche in Paris) with Eduard Troelsgård, and the first job in Troelsgård's archive. It is the Catholic church most directly connected to your Paris taste.
Active parish. Hvidovre is in the deprioritised south-west, but it is worth the detour. The address and opening hours are unverified.
sanktnikolaj.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 10); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

p: Consecrated 1961; the parish was established in 1967. The architecture is undocumented in the sources consulted.
Active. Treat it as a lead to scout.
vorfrueherlev.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 11); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

p: A 25-storey, 120 m bed tower (one of Denmark's tallest buildings). It is joined to a fan-shaped concrete auditorium block and a four-storey treatment wing. Inside is Poul Gernes' complete polychrome scheme. According to poulgernes.dk, 4,500 doors to 3,700 rooms were painted in 21 colours, with 65 km of pink skirting board; the towers are colour-coded (cool to the north, warm to the south).

Competition won by Gehrdt Bornebusch, Max Brüel and Jørgen Selchau; built 1965–76. The tower combines slipformed in-situ concrete with precast elements. The top floors stayed unused until 2007. It is on InnovaConcrete's "100 from the 20th" list. Some original elements are already lost: KemiFOKUS reports that two of Gernes' four painted folding doors, which covered a bank and a hairdresser, were taken down around 2003 when those shops closed.
Working hospital; the foyer is public during normal hours.
herlevhosp.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 12); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

p: A rigid modular grid split into four quadrants by two axes. The standard buildings are in yellow brick with black window bands, and a forest belt was planted so the campus reads as "a town in a clearing".

Eva and Nils Koppel, with landscape architects Edith and Ole Nørgård. Built 1961–74 on the former Lundtofte airfield and officially inaugurated on 17 May 1974; it is Denmark's largest single university complex. DTU publishes an 11-stop audio architecture route.
Open campus. Note that it is mostly brick, not concrete.
dtu.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 13); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

p: Karen and Ebbe Clemmensen's listed sports and pool complex: swimming hall 1966–69, ball halls 1970–72, listed 1998, with a 2001 extension by Entasis.

Renovation runs from 1 July 2026 to 2 January 2028. The 50 m pool and baby pool are closed, and Entrance A is closed until 2028. The 25 m, children's and diving pools stay open with changed hours. Tiles, the movable pool floor, ventilation and saunas are being replaced, so the original surfaces may change.
kildeskov.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 14); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

p: A 15-storey office tower of concrete with aluminium and glass curtain walls; the remaining studio buildings have been converted into student housing.

Built for Danmarks Radio from 1959 into the 1960s, designed by Mogens Boertmann at Vilhelm Lauritzens Tegnestue. It produced most of Danish TV until DR left in 2006–07. The tower was listed in 1998, but the studios were not, and some ancillary buildings were demolished. Nearly all the original drawings were thrown away during that demolition.
NCC is replacing the concrete and aluminium-and-glass façade for PensionDanmark, with completion expected in early 2027. The original skin is disappearing now.
tvbyen.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 15); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

p: A triangular fort sunk into the ridge, with only armoured turrets and domes showing above the glacis (the sloping earth bank in front). There is a dry moat, throat caponiers (flanking galleries at the rear), a separate salient caponier in concrete at the tip, and eight chimney stacks on the roof.
Built 1891–93 on the Nordfronten (the 1880s–90s northern fortification line); the command flag was raised on 20 December 1892. Fortunfortets Venner (the friends' association) give guided tours.

Casemates are normally locked; the outside can be reached from Fortunfortvej, Dyrehavegårdsvej or the Dyrehaven gate. It opens on Befæstningsdagen (last Sunday of September), so next opening is about September 2027.
fortun.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 16); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

p: A triangular sunken fort core, 172 m × 70 m, inside a villa road literally named Glaciset after the old earthwork. There are iron gates and shutters, and the moat is now a green.
Built 1888–92 and decommissioned 1920. The buyer immediately divided the glacis into villa plots. Contamination is registered on the site (regional soil pollution register).

Closed except for Befæstningsdagen and occasional evening tours by Fæstningskanalens Venner. Time-sensitive context: a dispensation for a new house at Glaciset 47 was granted on 5 October 2026, with the appeal period running to 3 November 2026.
lyngbyfort.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 17); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

p: A wet moat and bridge, the casemate building in the great traverse (the central earth-covered bank), the rangefinder entrance, and twelve 29 cm M/1910 howitzers still in their original positions.
Coastal battery of 1883–86, rebuilt as a coastal fort in 1910–12. Now part of Charlottenlund Strandpark.
Grounds are open; there is a campsite and restaurant on site (hours not checked).
charlottenlundfort.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 18); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

p: A preserved ammunition magazine with "HVIDØRE" over the entrance, surrounded by houses. The previous owners added fake brick walls, an oak gate, a sentry box and Belgian cannons.
Built 1892 as the right-wing coastal battery of the land fortifications, with four 17 cm guns, and decommissioned in 1922.
Private; a local historian reports "Adgang for uvedkommende strengt forbudt" (no unauthorised entry). View from Rosavej only.
hvidore.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 19); pin from the report, approximate.

p: Only the throat (rear) front facing Hvidørevej survives.
Built 1887–92 as the main work of the roughly 700 m Christiansholm line. Its "kvindekanoner" (women's cannons) were funded by patriotic women. It was divided into villa plots and roads after 1920.
Viewable from the street.
christiansholm.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 20); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

p: A grassy elongated mound measuring 300 × 170 m.

Built 1913–16 and closed 1968–69. DR reports that in 1969 the fort was handed to Jægersborg Skovdistrikt (the state forest district), which covered it with 300,000 tonnes of earth. For *Alt forladt* (DR2, broadcast 8 January 2013) DR dug 8 m down to the entrance and found the interior intact.
The mound is free to walk over; there is no interior access. A "buried ruin".
taarbaekfort.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 21); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

tinghojbat.t: Tinghøj Battery and the TV mast
p: Built 1887–88 and complete in 1891. It is a protected monument, but the moat is partly filled in and built over, and the site has been used for hazardous storage and is partly contaminated.
Private, and there is no access. A long-announced plan with the municipality to open it is unverified.

The 206.5 m Gladsaxe TV mast stands on the same site: Denmark's first TV transmissions went out from here, which makes the battery, TV-Byen and the reservoir one media-and-infrastructure cluster. (Report site 29, merged here because the two share a fence.)
tinghojbat.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 22); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

p: A civil-defence regional command bunker under Bernstorffsparken, now a youth music venue with about 14–15 rehearsal rooms, a studio and a 150-capacity concert room.
Built 1953 as the Østre Landsdelskommando central for Civilforsvaret (civil defence, not the military) and enlarged in 1971–74 to about 1,035–1,100 m²; sources differ on the area.
Open 08–24 for users aged 15–25. The public can attend concerts. No heritage tours were found for 2026.
musikbunker.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 23); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

p: A list dated 22 May 1944 planned 111 shelters for 50, 100 or 150 people; 43 were built. The Strandvejen/Ahlmanns Allé shelter was opened in 2013 for the first time since 1945 and now stores food for a restaurant.
Mostly sealed or reused. Whether the Ericavej shelter still physically exists is unverified. These are good "found object" stops at most.
gentofteshelter.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 24); pin from the report, approximate.

p: A Nike air-defence battery for Copenhagen from 1959 to 1981, one of four (with Kongelunden, Sigerslev and Tune). It was taken off readiness first; the final Nike parade was held on 1 March 1983.

A 2016 hiking account (not an official source) reports "adgang forbudt" and surviving remains. Current ownership and access are unverified. Do not confuse it with the separate radar station at Gunderødvej 33.
gunderod.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 25); pin from the report, approximate.

p: Two grass-covered plateaus over 10 underground reservoirs, totalling 10 ha. There are 20 small domed access towers in concrete, copper and steel with porthole-like windows, a hall building, a manager's house, a gothic-modernist timber tool shed and the striking valve building II (1943). Each reservoir has 264 mushroom columns, one of the earliest uses of flat-slab design.

By Poul Holsøe and Ib Lunding for the city architect's department, built 1928–59 in stages. It is Denmark's largest drinking-water installation, listed in 2000, and on InnovaConcrete's "100 from the 20th" list. The four 1951 water towers on Vandtårnsvej were demolished in 2015; only the base of one survives, as a pumping station.
Fenced and not publicly accessible; view from Vandtårnsvej.
tinghojres.s: Research report copenhagen-research-1b-deep.md (site 26); pin checked against Google Places, 23 Oct 2026.

p: Ib Lunding's sculptural functionalist tower, which preceded Tinghøj.

p: A huge reinforced-concrete power station clad in red brick, visible across Nordhavn and Svanemøllebugten. Sources disagree on its size: By & Havn gives 21,000 m², Dansk Byudvikling 22,000 m² and Licitationen 26,000 m².
Built 1947–53 by Københavns Belysningsvæsen (the city's lighting and power utility) to Louis Hygom's design. It burned coal until 1985, then gas, and production ended in 2023.

Closed and handed to By & Havn (the city's port and development company). According to Dansk Byudvikling, Bygnings- og udviklingsfonden DTM 4.0 is running a three-team architecture competition, with a budget of DKK 660 million (excluding VAT, 2026 prices), to convert it into Danmarks Tekniske Museum. The interior is not accessible. See it now, before conversion.

NR.name: Nørrebro to Ryvangen: Assistens, Panum and Bohr
NR.when: Ryvangen closes at 16:00 in October (15:00 from November), so end there by 15:00.
NR.summary: The rail-trail bridge, the cemetery of Kierkegaard, Andersen and Bohr, the brutalist Panum, Bohr's Auditorium A, the listed kiosk, a sea-mark church, then the execution ground at Ryvangen. About 8 km; bike it if you can.

NR.name: Frederiksberg and Vesterbro: Shellhus to Vestre Kirkegård
NR.when: Coffee at Josty (Tue–Sun, kitchen to 15:00). On Sat 31 Oct end at Vestre Kirkegård for 'De Dødes Dag' (14–17).
NR.summary: The Gestapo HQ site and the school hit by mistake in the same raid, Lenin's lodging, Kierkegaard's café in Frederiksberg Gardens, the lab that gave us pH, Denmark's largest cemetery and a locomotive workshop. About 5.5 km. New in 1.1: Enghave Church's concrete bell tower, and Schlegel's Søndermark crematorium as an add-on.

NR.name: Lyngby and Gentofte: concrete church, fort and Mariebjerg
NR.when: Weekend, for Garderhøjfortet (10:30–16). Sun 25 Oct the gun fires at 12:00. Bike or S-train between stops.
NR.summary: Denmark's first concrete church, the biggest 1880s ring fort, Brandt's grid of grave rooms, Hadid's wing at Ordrupgaard and the kiosk at Bakken. About 8 km. New in 1.1: Kildeskovshallen and the Cold War Musikbunkeren as add-ons.

NR.name: Bagsværd, Farum and Værløse by bike
NR.when: Tuesday is the one day both Bagsværd Church (10–14) and Hangar 2 (9–14) are open; or Sunday for the church and Saturday for the hangar.
NR.summary: An early concrete fort, Utzon's cloud vault, the corten megastructure at Farum, then the runway and shelters of the Cold War airbase. About 16 km by bike.

NR.name: Western suburbs: Exner, Vestvolden, the prison and Rømer
NR.when: Weekend for the prison tours (12:00 or 14:30, book). The churches open on weekdays only, so you get their exteriors.
NR.summary: The Exners' brick cave at Islev, the Nike command bunker in Vestvolden, Glostrup's crematorium, the closed Vridsløselille Prison, another Exner church and Rømer's observatory in the woods. About 17 km; bike or S-train.

NR.name: Amager by bike: Amagerbanen to the Nike sites
NR.when: Daylight. Kongelundsfortet is open 08–20. About 21 km, flat.
NR.summary: The old Amager railway, Kastrup Fort, Dragør's last water posts and its fort, then the Nike radar fort at Kongelunden and the missile magazines on the common.

NR.name: Køge Bay: Avedøre, ARKEN and Mosede
NR.when: Mosede Fort Tue–Fri 11–15, Sat–Sun 11–16; free intro tour 12:00. S-train along the coast.
NR.summary: The walled welfare town of Avedøre, the concrete ark of a museum on the beach, then the First World War fort and museum.

NR.name: North Zealand: royal milestones to Gilleleje
NR.when: Car or train. Gilleleje's plaques are outdoors; check the church if you want the loft.
NR.summary: Two of the King's Road milestones and the 1584 paved road, the sealed nuclear bunker in the forest, then Gilleleje's October 1943 trail.

NR.name: Malmö: the quarry and Lewerentz
NR.when: Lewerentz's kiosk closes at 17:00, so finish at the cemetery by 16:30.
NR.summary: The 65 m deep lime quarry from its rim, the 1901 power station that is now Moderna Museet, then Östra kyrkogården and Lewerentz's last building.

NR.name: Lund and Klippan
NR.when: Be at the cathedral for 12:00 (Sun 13:00) or 15:00. Klippan is about 1 h north; the church is open to 18:00.
NR.summary: The 600-year-old automaton clock, Strindberg's morning walk in the botanical garden, then Lewerentz's St Petri, where no brick was cut.

NR.name: Bispebjerg and Bellahøj: the crematorium dome, the first high-rises and Tingbjerg
NR.when: Daytime. The cemetery is open 7–19. Bellahøj Syd is being stripped (go soon); Husumvold Church is open Tue–Fri mornings.
NR.summary: The old crematorium dome at Bispebjerg Torv, Denmark's largest crematorium and cemetery axis, the 1950s point houses on Bellahøj, Holger Jensen's Husumvold church and Steen Eiler Rasmussen's Tingbjerg. About 6 km; good by bike.

NR.name: Gladsaxe and Herlev: TV-Byen, the reservoir domes, Høje Gladsaxe and Herlev Hospital
NR.when: Daytime, by bike. The reservoir and battery are fenced (view from Vandtårnsvej and Isbanevej). The hospital foyer is public.
NR.summary: DR's old TV tower, the domed access towers of Tinghøj reservoir, the battery under the TV mast, the slab wall of Høje Gladsaxe and the 120 m hospital tower with Poul Gernes' colours. About 6 km.

NR.name: Lyngby: Lyngbyfortet, the DTU grid and Fortunfortet
NR.when: Any time in daylight. Both forts open inside only on Befæstningsdagen (last Sunday of September).
NR.summary: The sunken fort inside a villa road called Glaciset, the Koppels' 1960s campus grid, and Fortunfortet on the edge of Dyrehaven. About 5 km; close to home.

NR.name: The Øresund coast: Charlottenlund Fort to the buried Taarbæk Fort
NR.when: Daylight. Charlottenlund Fort is open; Hvidøre and Christiansholm are private, seen from the street.
NR.summary: The coastal fort with its 29 cm howitzers in place, two batteries swallowed by villa gardens, then into Dyrehaven to the grassy mound that hides Taarbæk Fort. About 6 km along Strandvejen.
